Section 2 — Impact (evaluation weight: 30%)

This section addresses the three Impact sub-criteria as they apply to a 24-month European Fellowship (EF) under call HORIZON-MSCA-2026-PF-01-01, hosted at Eötvös Loránd University (ELTE), Budapest, Faculty of Informatics, Institute of Cartography and Geoinformatics, with Dr. Rositsa Cholakova as the fellow and Dr. András Jung as supervisor. The Impact account below is organised around the project's four confirmed impact streams — IMP-1 (Scientific advance in probabilistic multi-sensor crop-water-state estimation), IMP-2 (Economic and societal impact: water-use efficiency and farm resilience), IMP-3 (Environmental co-benefit through landscape-compatible sensing) and IMP-4 (Advancement of the researcher's career and the European Research Area) — and is mapped in full against the seven call expected impacts (EI-01 through EI-07) through the seven confirmed impact pathways (PWY-EI-01 through PWY-EI-07) produced by Phase 5 of the orchestration workflow. All impact claims are calibrated to the project's confirmed research-prototype TRL target (TRL 3–4, RQ10) and the 24-month European Fellowship timeline; the project does not assert operational deployment, commercial uptake at scale, or quantified field-scale water savings during the fellowship.


2.1  Career perspectives and employability of the researcher

2.1.1  The researcher and her trajectory into the fellowship

Dr. Rositsa Cholakova is a plant physiologist specialising in non-destructive techniques for the evaluation of abiotic and biotic plant stress and crop monitoring. She holds a current position at the Maritsa Vegetable Crops Research Institute, Bulgarian Agricultural Academy, Plovdiv, Bulgaria, and her career spans approximately four years post-PhD. Her doctoral thesis (summa cum laude, 2020) addressed the non-destructive evaluation of the physiological status of drought-stressed tomato plants (doi:10.2139/ssrn.5492527); she has further peer-reviewed work on maize chilling-stress photosynthesis and biostimulants. This disciplinary identity — plant physiologist with deep expertise in non-destructive stress phenotyping and in tomato specifically — is not a generic science background. It is the load-bearing competence for the project's biological ground-truth engine: the confirmed decision on validation measurement (RQ4: chlorophyll fluorescence, stomatal conductance, canopy/leaf temperature and spectral reflectance as ground truth) is precisely the instrumentation in which the fellow holds specialist expertise, and the confirmed crop choice (RQ1: tomato) matches her PhD subject matter exactly. The fellow-to-host knowledge-transfer direction is therefore scientifically indispensable to the project, not incidental.

The fellowship represents a deliberate disciplinary leap. The fellow moves from a plant-physiology and crop-monitoring research environment (Maritsa Vegetable Crops Research Institute) into a geoinformatics and remote-sensing environment (ELTE, Faculty of Informatics, Institute of Cartography and Geoinformatics), acquiring expertise in probabilistic Earth observation, multi-sensor data fusion, Bayesian calibration and uncertainty quantification that she does not currently hold and that would be unavailable in a plant-physiology-only host environment. This disciplinary expansion does not dilute her plant-physiology identity; it creates a distinctive cross-disciplinary profile coupling non-destructive stress phenotyping with probabilistic remote sensing that is rare in both the precision agriculture and the Earth observation research communities.

The Bulgaria-to-Hungary move satisfies the MSCA-PF mobility rule. As an intra-EU mobility, the fellowship is classified as a European Fellowship, and 24 months is the confirmed duration.

2.1.2  Supervision: structure and interdisciplinary complementarity

Dr. András Jung, as supervisor at Eötvös Loránd University (ELTE), Budapest, provides a supervisory profile directly matched to the fellowship's interdisciplinary aims. In his role as Deputy Head of the Institute of Cartography and Geoinformatics, he oversees the host group's geoinformatics and remote-sensing research infrastructure. As Head of the Multisensor-Drone-Fusion Working Group (project ELTE TKP2021-NVA-29), he anchors the technical direction on multi-sensor Earth observation and hyperspectral-drone fusion that constitutes the host-to-fellow transfer direction. His co-founding of Cubert GmbH (hyperspectral cameras) and Brightic Research, together with his habilitations in both Computer Science and Crop Sciences, give him disciplinary breadth spanning the computational and agricultural dimensions of this fellowship in a way that is uncommon in a single supervisor. The Crop Sciences habilitation in particular means that the host-to-fellow transfer of geoinformatics methods occurs within a supervisory relationship where the computational expertise is already contextualised against the agricultural domain the fellow is working in.

Supervision is structured around the Career Development Plan (D4-01, WP4: Training, supervision and two-way transfer of knowledge), which is jointly prepared by the supervisor and the fellow and submitted as a project deliverable at the start of the action (by month 3), then reviewed and updated during the fellowship. The Career Development Plan is the operative instrument for enacting the European Charter for Researchers principles of transparent supervision, clear mutual expectations, regular career review, and structured training. It covers the fellow's research objectives, training and career needs including transferable skills, teaching activities, publication plans and open science activities, in conformance with call scope requirement SR-04. Reviews at the interim and final stages of the fellowship ensure that the plan remains live rather than a start-of-action filing obligation.

2.1.3  Two-way transfer of knowledge: mechanism and evidence

The career-development impact of this fellowship rests on a two-way knowledge transfer that is structurally genuine: each transfer direction is independently necessary for the project to succeed, which means neither party is providing a peripheral courtesy contribution.

The fellow-to-host transfer direction carries the fellow's plant-physiology and non-destructive stress-phenotyping expertise into the ELTE geoinformatics group. This is the project's biological ground-truth engine: the validation protocol in WP3 (Field validation, ground truth and uncertainty calibration) is built around non-destructive physiological measurements of chlorophyll fluorescence, stomatal conductance, canopy/leaf temperature and spectral reflectance (RQ4) that represent the fellow's core specialist instrumentation. The host's geoinformatics group does not currently hold this competence; acquiring it through the fellowship — not just for this project but for ELTE's capacity in precision agriculture more broadly — is a genuine institutional gain documented in the Career Development Plan (D4-01) and evidenced at each periodic review.

The host-to-fellow transfer direction carries ELTE's remote-sensing, hyperspectral imaging and multisensor-drone fusion methods — under Dr. András Jung's supervision — into the fellow's practice. This is the diagnostic and probabilistic modelling architecture of the project: the fellow must develop competence in probabilistic machine learning, Bayesian multi-sensor calibration, and uncertainty propagation across an observation-to-decision pipeline to lead WP1 (Probabilistic multi-sensor diagnosis of the field state) and WP2 (Uncertainty-aware decision engine and demonstrator integration). These are competences the fellow does not currently hold at the level required by the project, and they are the ones that will constitute the fellowship's lasting contribution to the fellow's research toolkit.

The Career Development Plan (D4-01) formally documents both transfer directions as named and reviewable elements of the fellowship, and the KPI for the two-way transfer (KPI-02) requires that both directions are evidenced in CDP reviews by documented transfer events in each direction. The IMP-4 impact stream maps this mechanism to the call's expected impacts EI-01 (improved employability), EI-05 (alignment with the European Charter for Researchers) and EI-07 (new mind-sets through interdisciplinary experience), and to expected outcomes EO-01 (increased research and transferable skills), EO-02 (new mind-sets and approaches) and EO-04 (alignment with Charter principles).

2.1.4  Training: mandatory dimensions and project grounding

Training is organised around the MSCA-PF mandatory transferable-skills dimensions, as required by scope requirement SR-03, and each dimension is grounded directly in the project's research content rather than as generic add-on modules:

— Digital and AI skills, including the responsible use of generative AI: the project's probabilistic machine-learning modelling, Bayesian calibration and data-fusion pipelines provide a live development context for digital and AI competences, including the specific sub-competence of responsible use of generative AI tools in environmental modelling and scientific coding that SR-03 identifies by name.

— Knowledge valorisation and innovation and entrepreneurship: the project's demonstrator-oriented work (WP2: Uncertainty-aware decision engine and demonstrator integration) and the connection to the associated partner AgroVIR for farmer-facing feedback and testing constitute a concrete entrepreneurship and valorisation context within which the fellow learns to position a research prototype towards end-user uptake.

— Research integrity and good scientific conduct: the project's methodological heart — the honest uncertainty chain carried from observation to decision — provides a natural vehicle for research integrity training. Calibrated uncertainty reporting (RQ5: 90% prediction-interval coverage as the validation criterion) is itself an exercise in scientific honesty, and the open validation protocol and FAIR data release (D5-01 and D5-02, WP5) are research-integrity practices embedded in the project design.

— Open science and FAIR data stewardship: the Data Management Plan (D5-01, WP5: Dissemination, exploitation, communication and management) delivered by month 6, and the Dissemination and exploitation plan (D5-02, WP5) also delivered by month 6, constitute the operational open-science framework for the project. All primary research outputs — the Diagnostic model specification and calibration report (D1-01), the Decision engine and demonstrator software (D2-01) and the Field validation dataset and uncertainty calibration report (D3-01) — are committed to FAIR release.

2.1.5  Career perspectives and employability at the fellowship's end

The impact stream IMP-4 describes the consolidated career outcome: a cross-disciplinary research profile coupling plant physiology and non-destructive stress phenotyping with geoinformatics and probabilistic remote sensing, documented through peer-reviewed publication in an area the literature reports as underdeveloped, supported by an open-source demonstrator and a FAIR-compliant benchmark field-validation dataset, and enriched by a structured training programme across all MSCA-PF mandatory dimensions. This profile is distinctive in both the precision agriculture and the Earth observation research communities and positions the fellow for research leadership in either or both, or in the cross-disciplinary space between them.

Specific quantitative career targets — publication counts, training hours, thesis co-supervision figures, seminar counts, follow-on proposal deadlines — are deliberately not asserted in this proposal: none were operator-provided and none are to be invented. These targets are to be fixed in the Career Development Plan (D4-01) jointly with the supervisor at the start of the action, then updated at each review point. What can be asserted with confidence is that the project provides a credible basis for such targets to be set at a high level, because the research outputs from WP1, WP2 and WP3 represent a publication portfolio in a genuine literature gap, and the open code and data releases provide a durable scientific legacy beyond the fellowship. The contribution to EI-01 (improved employability within academia and beyond) and to the broader ERA-level EI-07 (new mind-sets enriching the European research culture) is grounded in this structural account of what the fellowship delivers, rather than in asserted numeric targets.


2.2  Dissemination, exploitation and communication

2.2.1  Open-science framework: Data Management Plan and Dissemination and exploitation plan

The project's dissemination, exploitation and communication strategy is anchored in two early-stage deliverables from WP5 (Dissemination, exploitation, communication and management): the Data Management Plan (D5-01, month 6) and the Dissemination and exploitation plan (D5-02, month 6). Both are led by the fellow and contributed to by Eötvös Loránd University (ELTE), Budapest, as host institution. The early delivery date — month 6, well before the primary research outputs from WP1, WP2 and WP3 are produced — ensures that the open-science framework is established prospectively rather than retrospectively applied to outputs already generated without an explicit DMP.

The Data Management Plan (D5-01) covers all primary project data assets: the sensor data (Sentinel-1 SAR, Sentinel-2 optical, PlanetScope, ERA5 meteorological reanalysis) assembled in WP1 (Probabilistic multi-sensor diagnosis of the field state); the uncertainty-aware AquaCrop calibration outputs and decision-engine records produced in WP2 (Uncertainty-aware decision engine and demonstrator integration); and the non-destructive physiological ground-truth data and validation records collected in WP3 (Field validation, ground truth and uncertainty calibration). FAIR compliance — findable, accessible, interoperable, reusable — is confirmed by D5-01 as the governing standard for all these data assets (KPI-11). The open-access policy commits all peer-reviewed publications to open-access routes in compliance with the Horizon Europe open-access mandate.

The Dissemination and exploitation plan (D5-02) identifies open-access dissemination routes for all primary research outputs of WP1, WP2 and WP3 (KPI-04), and documents the communication strategy to scientific and non-specialist audiences. Both documents are active through the fellowship: D5-02 is updated periodically as WP1 through WP3 outputs materialise.

2.2.2  Scientific dissemination: peer-reviewed publication

Open-access peer-reviewed publication is the primary scientific dissemination route. The project generates publishable results from three distinct scientific activity blocks. WP1 (Probabilistic multi-sensor diagnosis of the field state) produces the Diagnostic model specification and calibration report (D1-01, month 14), which documents the Route A and Route B probabilistic fusion architectures, the calibration methodology and the uncertainty-calibration evidence — constituting a novel scientific contribution to multi-sensor Bayesian crop-water-state estimation. WP2 (Uncertainty-aware decision engine and demonstrator integration) produces the Decision engine and demonstrator software (D2-01, month 20), which documents the uncertainty-aware AquaCrop calibration and the WUE-based counterfactual decision engine — a contribution to uncertainty-aware crop modelling and irrigation decision support. WP3 (Field validation, ground truth and uncertainty calibration) produces the Field validation dataset and uncertainty calibration report (D3-01, month 24), establishing whether the 90% prediction-interval coverage criterion (RQ5) is met on the Hungarian tomato farm validation set — a methodological validation result suitable for publication in its own right as a calibration study.

All publications arising from the project are committed to open-access routes. The target research community for scientific dissemination comprises multi-sensor fusion, probabilistic crop-water-state estimation and uncertainty-aware decision-support researchers in geoinformatics, remote sensing and precision agriculture; natural conference dissemination channels include ISPRS, IEEE IGARSS and precision agriculture-focused venues. Publications are anticipated from mid-project (following D1-01 delivery at month 14) through to the end of the fellowship, contingent on the validation protocol.

Open-access publication in this domain advances the call's expected outcome EO-03 (enhanced networking and communication capacities) and the call's expected impact EI-02 (increased and broadened R&I impact through enhanced networking and communication), as the fellow builds her international scientific network and brings the project's results to peer audiences. It also advances EI-04 (increased global attractiveness and reputation of ELTE and, by extension, of the ERA), because open publication addressing a documented literature gap — the empty real-time decision-support × PlanetScope cell of the reviewed gap matrix — elevates ELTE's visibility in the multi-sensor EO and uncertainty-quantification research community.

2.2.3  Open-source code and benchmark dataset release

Open-source code release under FAIR principles is the second major dissemination axis, and it carries particular weight in this project because the community need for end-to-end open implementations is genuine. Few openly available implementations currently link multi-sensor Earth observation, probabilistic crop-water-state estimation and irrigation decision optimisation in a reproducible, FAIR-compliant package. The project addresses this gap through three timed releases:

— Month 14: open code repository for the probabilistic fusion diagnostic code accompanying the Diagnostic model specification and calibration report (D1-01), covering the Route A and Route B implementations and the calibration framework. FAIR compliance confirmed by the Data Management Plan (D5-01) (KPI-10).

— Month 20: open-source software release of the Decision engine and demonstrator software (D2-01), covering the uncertainty-aware AquaCrop calibration, the counterfactual irrigation simulation over weather ensembles, and the WUE-based recommendation logic — as an openly licensed, replicable end-to-end decision-support prototype at TRL 3–4 (KPI-06).

— Month 24: open FAIR release of the Field validation dataset and uncertainty calibration report (D3-01) from Hungarian tomato farms, assigned a DOI or open repository reference (KPI-08). This dataset captures non-destructive physiological ground truth (chlorophyll fluorescence, stomatal conductance, canopy/leaf temperature, spectral reflectance) from confirmed Hungarian tomato farm sites accessed via AgroVIR, with matched multi-sensor EO data streams. It constitutes an internationally reproducible benchmark for probabilistic multi-sensor crop-water diagnosis, a resource that outlives the fellowship and supports ELTE's international reputation in precision agriculture sensing.

These three releases directly advance EI-03 (stronger R&I capacity and knowledge transfer at ELTE and in the broader community) and EI-04 (increased attractiveness and reputation of ELTE and the ERA) by providing durable, openly accessible research infrastructure rather than results locked in publications alone.

2.2.4  Communication to non-specialist audiences: AgroVIR and farmer engagement

The associated partner AgroVIR (Hungary) provides the channel through which the project's research connects to the tomato farming community in Hungary during the fellowship itself. AgroVIR's confirmed scope is farmer access, field validation support and iterative feedback, but not ownership or operation of the demonstrator tool. This scoping is deliberate: AgroVIR's engagement gives the research prototype real-world grounding even at TRL 3–4, and its iterative feedback during WP3 (Field validation, ground truth and uncertainty calibration) informs the demonstrator's design rather than constituting a deployment relationship. The Dissemination and exploitation plan (D5-02) formalises this communication channel alongside the academic and open-science routes.

The tomato-farming context also provides a natural non-specialist communication opportunity: the project's observable output — an irrigation recommendation with a stated confidence range — is comprehensible to a grower audience in a way that a Bayesian posterior is not. Communication materials addressed to farmer audiences can be built around the recommendation layer rather than the probabilistic machinery, and D5-02 provides the framework for developing these materials.

2.2.5  Feedback into teaching and education at ELTE

Elte's position as a university host creates a specific exploitation route that extends the project's open-science dissemination into higher education. The research outputs from WP1 and WP2 — the probabilistic fusion diagnostic model and the uncertainty-aware decision engine — represent concrete, teachable advances in Bayesian multi-sensor fusion and crop-water state estimation. ELTE's Faculty of Informatics delivers geoinformatics, remote sensing and precision agriculture curricula to MSc and PhD students; the project's open-source code and FAIR-compliant data released under the Data Management Plan (D5-01) can be incorporated directly into ELTE's teaching as laboratory exercises, case studies or reproducible workflows. Curriculum integration is envisaged from month 18 onwards, following D1-01 delivery at month 14 and D2-01 delivery at month 20, with FAIR compliance confirmed by D5-01 (KPI-10, KPI-11). This pathway directly realises the call's expected outcome EO-08 (regular feedback of research results into teaching and education at participating organisations) and expected impact EI-06.

2.2.6  Intellectual property rights strategy

No patent protection is sought. The project's primary outputs — scientific publications, the Diagnostic model specification and calibration report (D1-01), the Decision engine and demonstrator software (D2-01) and the Field validation dataset and uncertainty calibration report (D3-01) — are research artefacts intended for open dissemination under FAIR principles and permissive open-source licences. This IPR posture is consistent with the project's confirmed TRL target (TRL 3–4, RQ10): at research-prototype stage, impact is realised through open scientific dissemination, community uptake and ELTE's research capacity building rather than commercial exclusivity. The approach is also consistent with the MSCA-PF instrument's emphasis on knowledge transfer (EI-03) and ERA capacity (EI-04). IP arrangements that might arise from any post-fellowship exploitation activity are not determined by this proposal and are left to post-project negotiation involving ELTE and any downstream partners.


2.3  Scientific, societal and economic impact

2.3.1  Overview of the impact architecture

The project's scientific, societal and economic impact is organised into three research-content impact streams: IMP-1 (Scientific advance in probabilistic multi-sensor crop-water-state estimation), IMP-2 (Economic and societal impact: water-use efficiency and farm resilience for tomato horticulture) and IMP-3 (Environmental co-benefit through landscape-compatible sensing via Route B). A fourth stream, IMP-4 (Advancement of the researcher's career and the European Research Area), is addressed in sub-section 2.1 and is cross-referenced below in its mapping to the call expected impacts. All three research-content impact streams are grounded in the project's confirmed methodology, confirmed research decisions (RQ1 through RQ10) and confirmed work package structure, and their magnitude is proportionate to the 24-month European Fellowship timeline and the TRL 3–4 research-prototype scope.

2.3.2  IMP-1: Scientific advance in probabilistic multi-sensor crop-water-state estimation and irrigation decision support

The scientific impact claim of this project rests on a specific, defended literature gap and a specific, narrow novelty, not on broad assertions about the importance of satellite data for agriculture.

The gap is identified by a systematic review of 50 studies on multi-sensor crop water stress monitoring, whose research-gap matrix (METH-SOTA-007) shows counts falling sharply along two gradients: as sensor integration deepens, and as the task moves from status detection to optimisation to real-time decision support. The two gradients converge on a single empty cell — Real-Time Decision Support × PlanetScope — that the project targets. Genuine probabilistic precedents exist and are respected in the novelty argument: Bayesian Maximum Entropy drought fusion, copula-based drought/irrigation scheduling, dynamic Bayesian networks and MF-FusionNet are all acknowledged prior work. The defended novelty, argued narrowly against these precedents, is the end-to-end coupling of three elements that no reviewed precedent combines: learned multimodal fusion directly from multiple sensor streams; explicit probabilistic crop-water-state estimation outputs carrying honest uncertainty; and water-use-efficiency-oriented irrigation decision optimisation drawing on those probabilistic estimates through a counterfactual simulation over weather ensembles. The claim is deliberately confined to this combination, and it is defensible only if the uncertainty chain is maintained honestly from observation to decision.

The scientific advance is realised through three work packages and three corresponding deliverables:

— WP1 (Probabilistic multi-sensor diagnosis of the field state) → Diagnostic model specification and calibration report (D1-01, month 14): documents the Route A direct probabilistic fusion architecture (fusing Sentinel-1 SAR, Sentinel-2 optical, PlanetScope, ERA5 meteorological and field-observation data into a calibrated posterior for root-zone soil moisture and crop water status, RQ3) and the Route B homogeneous patch proxy architecture (the project's primary route per RQ2: sidestep the sub-pixel resolution problem by reading a nearby covarying patch whose biology co-varies with the target tomato crop), together with the calibration methodology and calibration evidence.

— WP2 (Uncertainty-aware decision engine and demonstrator integration) → Decision engine and demonstrator software (D2-01, month 20): implements uncertainty-aware AquaCrop calibration retaining an honest parameter posterior rather than collapsing to a single overconfident parameter set, runs counterfactual irrigation simulations over weather ensembles, and implements the WUE-based recommendation logic (RQ6) that steers toward the irrigation option with the best expected water-use efficiency under uncertainty.

— WP3 (Field validation, ground truth and uncertainty calibration) → Field validation dataset and uncertainty calibration report (D3-01, month 24): establishes whether the uncertainty calibration criterion (RQ5: 90% prediction intervals containing the ground truth approximately 90% of the time on the validation set) is met, using non-destructive physiological ground truth from Hungarian tomato farms (chlorophyll fluorescence, stomatal conductance, canopy/leaf temperature and spectral reflectance, RQ4) accessed via AgroVIR. Route B's covariation assumption is proven, not assumed, by the co-located seasonal measurement campaign (RQ9), which measures the target tomato crop and the proxy patch simultaneously and demonstrates statistical covariation.

The pilot success criterion (RQ7) — the RQ5 calibration target met on the validation set — is the pivotal scientific quality gate. It makes the scientific quality claim defensible in a way that accuracy percentages without calibration evidence are not: a model can be accurate on average while being systematically overconfident, and the calibration criterion distinguishes these cases. The calibration evidence in D3-01 is therefore the central scientific contribution of the validation phase, not a routine evaluation appendix.

The indicators for IMP-1 are: (a) open-access publication establishing the end-to-end probabilistic fusion-to-decision framework (KPI-05, KPI-06); (b) demonstrated honest uncertainty propagation from observation to decision, evidenced by calibration results in D3-01 against the RQ5 criterion; and (c) novelty defended against the reviewed precedents, documented in the publications. The timeline for IMP-1 realisation runs from month 14 (D1-01) through months 20 and 24 (D2-01, D3-01), with publications from mid-project contingent on validation protocol completion.

IMP-1 maps to the call's expected impact EI-02 (pathway PWY-EI-02: increased R&I impact through the project's substantive novel outputs disseminated via WP5), EI-03 (pathway PWY-EI-03: strengthened R&I capacity at ELTE in multi-sensor EO and Bayesian calibration) and EI-04 (pathway PWY-EI-04: ELTE's international visibility elevated through open publication addressing the literature gap and through the benchmark dataset D3-01), and to expected outcomes EO-06 and EO-07.

2.3.3  IMP-2: Economic and societal impact — water-use efficiency and farm resilience for tomato horticulture

Row-crop horticulture, including tomato cultivation, faces increasing water-use pressure under climate change. Irrigation decisions made under uncertainty impose both water waste (irrigating when not necessary) and yield risk (under-irrigating when necessary), and the cost of each error is not symmetric. The project addresses this by moving the decision frame from monitoring — what is the current stress status? — to economically grounded decision support — given uncertain future weather and our uncertain current diagnosis, what is the best irrigation choice for water-use efficiency?

The project's confirmed decision objective is water-use efficiency (WUE, RQ6), explicitly selected rather than yield alone or profit, because WUE captures the efficiency of water conversion to crop output, which is the relevant quantity when water is the scarce resource. Framing the recommendation as WUE-optimised rather than yield-maximising is both scientifically appropriate and societally aligned: it incentivises efficient use rather than maximum extraction. The framework is kept open to profit-based or drought-risk objective formulations as alternative instantiations of the same architecture.

The project's output on this dimension is the Uncertainty-aware AquaCrop decision engine (OUT-2) and its integration in the Decision engine and demonstrator software (D2-01, month 20). The demonstrator presents WUE-optimised irrigation recommendations alongside their uncertainty, giving the farmer or agronomist a recommendation and a stated confidence range rather than a point recommendation with no uncertainty disclosure. The demonstrator is a research prototype (TRL 3–4, RQ10); it is not a commercial product and no operational deployment or quantified field-scale water savings are claimed during the fellowship.

The pathway from prototype to societal impact is staged and grounded. AgroVIR (Hungary), the confirmed associated partner, provides farmer access, field validation support and iterative testing feedback throughout WP3. This engagement gives the demonstrator real-world grounding at TRL 3–4, ensures the recommendation interface design is informed by practical farming contexts, and begins building the relationships through which a subsequent operational deployment — by a commercial actor or a public extension service, after further development beyond TRL 3–4 — could occur. AgroVIR's scope is farmer access and feedback, not ownership or operation of the tool.

The verifiable indicators for IMP-2 are: (i) irrigation recommendations scored explicitly by WUE under uncertainty, documented in D2-01's decision-engine specification (KPI-06); (ii) the demonstrator exercised on the full observation-to-decision pipeline with uncertainty-aware recommendations, evidenced by D2-01 delivery at month 20; and (iii) pilot success defined as the RQ5 calibration target met on the validation set (RQ7), confirming that the WUE recommendations are built on calibrated rather than overconfident probabilistic estimates, evidenced in D3-01 at month 24.

IMP-2 maps to the call's expected impacts EI-02 (pathway PWY-EI-02: the decision-engine and demonstrator outputs are substantive R&I content worth disseminating to the agricultural technology and farming communities) and EI-03 (pathway PWY-EI-03: the decision-engine outputs increase ELTE's research output in precision agriculture decision support). The economic and societal impact at the farming level is not yet asserted as realised; it is asserted as enabled by the validated research prototype, which is the appropriate claim for a 24-month European Fellowship at TRL 3–4.

2.3.4  IMP-3: Environmental co-benefit through landscape-compatible sensing

The project's primary diagnostic route — Route B, the homogeneous patch proxy (confirmed as the project's main route per RQ2) — carries an environmental co-benefit that derives from its methodological logic. Route B sidesteps the sub-pixel resolution problem inherent in reading heterogeneous agricultural landscapes with coarse-resolution satellite instruments by instead identifying a nearby, spectrally and biologically homogeneous patch — typically semi-natural or extensively managed vegetation — whose biology covaries with the target tomato crop. The coarse satellite pixel can read this patch cleanly, without the mixing problems that require sub-pixel disaggregation. The implication is that the sensing approach depends on the existence of such patches in the agricultural landscape: their presence is methodologically valuable, not merely tolerable from an ecological management standpoint.

This creates an alignment between the method and landscape sustainability. Keeping semi-natural or extensively managed patches in the agricultural landscape is consistent with biodiversity-compatible land management practices, and Route B provides a remote-sensing argument for that practice that is independent of the usual regulatory or conservation framing: the patch is a precision-agriculture asset. Route B's Control Stand Variant (METH-ROUTE-003) extends this further, deliberately planting a covarying species as a designed proxy sensor so that covariation can be measured rather than assumed — a methodological extension that reinforces the incentive for retaining or establishing compatible plant communities in the agricultural setting.

The environmental co-benefit (IMP-3) is validated by the co-located seasonal measurement campaign (RQ9), which simultaneously measures the target tomato crop and the proxy patch to establish statistical covariation empirically rather than assuming it. Route B's ecological co-benefit is articulated as the methodology's strategic upside in the literature — the methodology works better when the landscape contains compatible patches, so the methodology creates an argument for maintaining them — and this strategic framing is grounded in the Route B methodology (METH-ROUTE-002, source_grounded) and the operator-confirmed decisions (RQ2, RQ9). The same proxy logic could in principle be applied to other row-crop contexts where matched homogeneous patches exist, which is a further scalability dimension noted but not asserted as an impact claim within the scope of this project.

The verifiable indicators for IMP-3 are: Route B validated as a landscape-compatible sensing strategy via the co-located covariation test (RQ9), documented in D3-01; and the ecological co-benefit articulated as part of the methodology's strategic upside in the project's publications.

IMP-3 maps to the call's societal and environmental dimension within EI-02 (broader R&I impact of the project's methodological innovation in landscape-compatible sensing).

2.3.5  Consolidated impact pathway mapping: alignment with all seven call expected impacts

The Phase 5 impact architecture confirms that all seven call expected impacts (EI-01 through EI-07) are covered by project-specific pathways (coverage_status = Covered for all seven). The mapping is reproduced here in consolidated form for evaluator clarity:

EI-01 — Improved employability and career prospects of MSCA postdoctoral fellows (pathway PWY-EI-01): realised through IMP-4 via WP4 (Training, supervision and two-way transfer of knowledge) and D4-01 (Career Development Plan). The distinctive cross-disciplinary profile coupling plant physiology with geoinformatics, documented in the Career Development Plan and evidenced through the two-way transfer, broadens the fellow's career options in precision agriculture and Earth observation. KPI-01 (D4-01 submitted by month 3, covering all mandatory MSCA-PF training dimensions) and KPI-02 (both transfer directions documented in CDP reviews) are the verifiable indicators. Call expected outcomes addressed: EO-01, EO-02.

EI-02 — Increased and broadened R&I impact through enhanced networking and communication (pathway PWY-EI-02): realised through IMP-1, IMP-2 and IMP-4 via WP1–WP5 and all six deliverables. The project's substantive scientific and economic outputs (probabilistic fusion framework, WUE decision engine, benchmark field-validation dataset) constitute meaningful R&I content; WP4 training develops communication competences; WP5 formalises dissemination channels under FAIR principles and open-access mandate. KPI-03 (D5-01 by month 6, covering all primary data assets) and KPI-04 (D5-02 by month 6, with open-access routes for WP1–WP3 primary outputs) are the verifiable indicators. Call expected outcome addressed: EO-03.

EI-03 — Stronger R&I capacity and output and better knowledge transfer among participating organisations (pathway PWY-EI-03): realised through IMP-1 and IMP-4 via WP1–WP4. The Diagnostic model specification and calibration report (D1-01) and Decision engine and demonstrator software (D2-01) directly increase ELTE's research output in multi-sensor EO, Bayesian calibration and uncertainty-aware crop modelling. The Career Development Plan (D4-01) formally structures the bi-directional transfer mechanism. KPI-05 (D1-01 by month 14 with calibration evidence) and KPI-06 (D2-01 by month 20 as open-source software) are the verifiable indicators. Call expected outcomes addressed: EO-05, EO-07.

EI-04 — Increased global attractiveness, visibility and reputation of the participating organisation and the ERA (pathway PWY-EI-04): realised through IMP-1 via WP1–WP3 and WP5. Open publication addressing the documented literature gap (real-time decision-support × PlanetScope cell, METH-SOTA-007) and the open FAIR release of the benchmark Hungarian tomato farm dataset (D3-01 with DOI, month 24) elevate ELTE's international citation footprint and reputation in the global multi-sensor EO and precision agriculture research community. KPI-07 (D5-02 by month 6 with international open-access venues for WP1 and WP2 outputs) and KPI-08 (D3-01 released as open benchmark dataset with DOI by month 24) are the verifiable indicators. Call expected outcome addressed: EO-06.

EI-05 — Increased alignment with the principles of the European Charter for Researchers (pathway PWY-EI-05): realised through IMP-4 via WP4 and D4-01. The jointly prepared Career Development Plan submitted as a project deliverable at the action's start and reviewed periodically enacts Charter principles of transparent supervision, clear mutual expectations, regular career review and equitable training access across all mandatory MSCA-PF training dimensions. KPI-09 (D4-01 assessed against Charter dimensions: supervision transparency, career-review schedule, training plan, research integrity module) is the verifiable indicator. Call expected outcome addressed: EO-04.

EI-06 — Regular feedback of research results into teaching and education at participating organisations (pathway PWY-EI-06): realised through IMP-1 via WP1, WP2 and WP5. The probabilistic fusion diagnostic model (D1-01) and the uncertainty-aware decision engine (D2-01) are concrete, teachable advances in Bayesian multi-sensor fusion for a university host with active geoinformatics and remote-sensing curricula; their open-source release under the DMP (D5-01) enables direct integration into ELTE's teaching from month 18. KPI-10 (open code repository established at D1-01 delivery; FAIR compliance confirmed by D5-01) and KPI-11 (D5-01 by month 6 covering all WP1–WP3 data assets) are the verifiable indicators. Call expected outcome addressed: EO-08.

EI-07 — New mind-sets and approaches through international, inter-sectoral and interdisciplinary experience (pathway PWY-EI-07): realised through IMP-4 and IMP-1 via WP4 (D4-01) and WP1 (D1-01). The fellowship's disciplinary pairing — plant-physiology expertise brought into a geoinformatics host — is the concrete mechanism through which new mind-sets are introduced. The two-way transfer, documented in the Career Development Plan (D4-01), and the methodological synthesis product of the interdisciplinary approach — the probabilistic fusion methodology (D1-01) that integrates physiological ground-truth design with Bayesian multi-sensor estimation — are the evidence that the new mind-set was not merely claimed but operationalised. KPI-12 (both transfer directions identified in D4-01 and evidenced at each review) and KPI-13 (D1-01 report evidences plant-physiology-grounded design choices within the probabilistic fusion architecture) are the verifiable indicators. Call expected outcome addressed: EO-02.

2.3.6  Sustainability and post-project continuity

Post-fellowship sustainability is grounded in three complementary mechanisms. First, Eötvös Loránd University (ELTE), Budapest retains the probabilistic fusion methodology, validated open-source code (D1-01, D2-01) and the benchmark field-validation dataset (D3-01) as open research infrastructure within the geoinformatics and remote sensing group of the Faculty of Informatics, Institute of Cartography and Geoinformatics, enabling continued use, extension and teaching by ELTE researchers and students beyond the fellowship period (IMP-1, EI-03, EI-06). Second, the FAIR release of all primary code and data assets under the Data Management Plan (D5-01) ensures that the global precision agriculture and Earth observation research community can build on and independently extend the results without dependence on the project's continued funding; this secures the scientific impact (IMP-1, IMP-2) as a durable public research infrastructure contribution rather than a time-limited project output. Third, the fellow's consolidated cross-disciplinary profile — coupling plant physiology and non-destructive stress phenotyping with geoinformatics and probabilistic remote sensing, documented in the Career Development Plan (D4-01) — sustains the two-way knowledge transfer relationship between the fellow and ELTE beyond the fellowship and enables continued collaboration, career development and research leadership in precision agriculture and Earth observation on both sides (IMP-4, EI-01, EI-07).

sub_sections.title: Credibility of the measures to enhance the career perspectives and employability of the researcher and contribution to his/her skills development
sub_sections.content:
2.1  Credibility of the measures to enhance the career perspectives and employability of the researcher and contribution to his/her skills development

The Impact criterion's first sub-criterion asks whether the project's career-development measures are specific, credible, and coherent with the researcher's starting position and career trajectory, and whether the proposed skills-development programme will make a defensible and lasting contribution to her future career inside and outside academia. The answer must go beyond listing training topics: it must demonstrate that the measures are grounded in the project's own research content, mutually reinforcing, and proportionate to the genuine disciplinary gap the fellowship is designed to fill.

This sub-section addresses that question in eight parts: (i) the fellow's current profile and the competences she brings to the fellowship; (ii) why the fellowship's disciplinary reorientation is career-decisive rather than incidental; (iii) the supervisor's profile and its relevance to the fellow's development; (iv) the Career Development Plan as the operative instrument of career development; (v) the two-way transfer of knowledge and its bilateral career-development significance; (vi) the specific measures targeting career development inside academia; (vii) the specific measures targeting career development outside academia; and (viii) the expected structural contribution of the fellowship's skills-development programme to the fellow's long-term career.


2.1.1  The fellow's current profile: a load-bearing specialist, not a generic early-career researcher

Dr. Rositsa Cholakova is a plant physiologist specialising in non-destructive techniques for the evaluation of abiotic and biotic plant stress and crop monitoring. She holds a current position at the Maritsa Vegetable Crops Research Institute, Bulgarian Agricultural Academy, Plovdiv, Bulgaria, and her career spans approximately four years post-PhD. Her doctoral thesis — completed summa cum laude in 2020, addressing the non-destructive evaluation of the physiological status of drought-stressed tomato plants (doi:10.2139/ssrn.5492527) — established a research identity that is specific rather than generic: plant physiology, non-destructive stress phenotyping, and tomato are the three defining elements of her prior published record. Her further peer-reviewed work encompasses maize chilling-stress photosynthesis and biostimulant effects on plant physiological responses, extending the non-destructive evaluation and stress-physiology core into related stress types and crop contexts.

This profile has two properties of central importance for the career-development analysis. First, it is already distinctive and internationally identifiable within a specific research niche. Dr. Cholakova is not a generalist early-career researcher seeking initial specialisation; she is a practising specialist with a track record in a well-defined methodological domain. This means the fellowship's career-development contribution must be assessed not as initiating a research career from scratch but as extending and repositioning an established specialist trajectory in a way that amplifies its future impact. Second, her existing expertise maps precisely onto the project's biological ground-truth requirements. The operator-confirmed decision on ground-truth measurement (RQ4: chlorophyll fluorescence, stomatal conductance, canopy/leaf temperature and spectral reflectance as ground truth) is exactly the instrumentation in which Dr. Cholakova holds specialist expertise, developed over her doctoral and post-doctoral career. The operator-confirmed crop (RQ1: tomato) is exactly the crop on which she completed her doctoral thesis. This correspondence is not coincidental: the project was designed so that the fellow's existing competences are structurally required by WP3 (Field validation, ground truth and uncertainty calibration). The fellow-to-host knowledge transfer is therefore scientifically load-bearing, not an optional enrichment activity.

The career observation that follows immediately from this profile is what it does not contain: probabilistic machine learning for Earth observation data, Bayesian multi-sensor calibration and uncertainty quantification, remote-sensing and hyperspectral imaging methodology, and geoinformatics data management. These are the host institution's strengths — the strengths of Eötvös Loránd University (ELTE), Budapest, Faculty of Informatics, Institute of Cartography and Geoinformatics, under Dr. András Jung — and they are precisely the competences that the host-to-fellow direction of the two-way transfer in WP4 (Training, supervision and two-way transfer of knowledge) is designed to deliver. The career development case rests on a genuinely asymmetric competence structure: the fellow offers irreplaceable physiological ground-truth expertise to the host, and the host offers irreplaceable probabilistic EO expertise to the fellow.


2.1.2  Why the disciplinary reorientation is career-decisive

The fellowship is not a continuation of the fellow's current research direction within a familiar institutional context. It is a deliberate and substantive disciplinary reorientation: from a plant-physiology and crop-monitoring research environment at the Maritsa Vegetable Crops Research Institute into the geoinformatics and remote-sensing research environment at Eötvös Loránd University (ELTE), Budapest, Faculty of Informatics, Institute of Cartography and Geoinformatics. The intra-EU mobility move from Plovdiv, Bulgaria to Budapest, Hungary qualifies the action as a European Fellowship under confirmed call binding HORIZON-MSCA-2026-PF-01-01, with a confirmed duration of 24 months.

In career-development terms, this reorientation has a specific structure and a specific consequence. The fellow is not abandoning her plant-physiology identity: she is extending it into a new methodological dimension that transforms what she can do as a researcher and what research problems she can credibly address. Before the fellowship, she can characterise plant water stress physiologically, in the field, using specialist non-destructive instruments. After the fellowship, she can also link those physiological measurements to probabilistic multi-sensor satellite-based diagnosis — fusing Sentinel-1 SAR, Sentinel-2 optical, PlanetScope and ERA5 meteorological reanalysis data into a calibrated posterior over the latent field state — and to uncertainty-aware crop-model-based decision support recommending irrigation choices by water-use efficiency. The resulting competence set couples physiological ground-truth design with probabilistic remote sensing and Bayesian calibration in a combination that is rare in both the precision agriculture and the Earth observation research communities, because few researchers have trained simultaneously in both.

This rarity is the fellowship's decisive career contribution. The precision agriculture research community requires researchers who understand both the physiological reality they are trying to measure and the probabilistic machinery through which remote sensors approximate that reality. The Earth observation community requires researchers who can validate probabilistic crop-water-state estimates against rigorous physiological ground truth rather than against coarser proxies. The fellow's post-fellowship profile addresses both needs from a base of demonstrated specialist performance in the physiological component, and from newly acquired specialist competence in the probabilistic EO component. This is the position the fellowship is designed to create, and it is not easily replicated by any alternative career path: a pure physiologist moving into EO does not automatically acquire the calibration and uncertainty-quantification depth that this project provides, and a pure EO researcher acquiring some plant physiology background does not acquire the non-destructive phenotyping instrument-design expertise that the fellow brings from her doctoral training.

The international dimension of the disciplinary reorientation further deepens the career impact. Basing the fellowship at Eötvös Loránd University (ELTE), Budapest integrates the fellow into the Hungarian and broader Central European geoinformatics and precision agriculture research community, building a research network that is complementary to her existing Bulgarian plant-physiology network and substantially broadens the geographic scope of her future collaboration and career options.


2.1.3  The supervisor's profile: matched to the interdisciplinary career-development aims

Dr. András Jung, as supervisor at Eötvös Loránd University (ELTE), Budapest, provides a supervisory profile directly and specifically matched to the fellowship's interdisciplinary career-development aims, not a profile of general scientific seniority.

His role as Deputy Head of the Institute of Cartography and Geoinformatics gives him institutional authority and resource visibility within the host organisation that are directly relevant to the fellow's integration into the geoinformatics and remote-sensing research community. His role as Head of the Multisensor-Drone-Fusion Working Group (project ELTE TKP2021-NVA-29) means that the host-to-fellow transfer of multisensor Earth observation and hyperspectral imaging methods occurs under the direct supervisory authority of the researcher who leads ELTE's active programme in exactly that methodological domain — not under a supervisor who manages that programme at a distance or supervises it secondarily.

His co-founding of Cubert GmbH, a manufacturer of hyperspectral cameras, and Brightic Research, provides a concrete and personal entrepreneurship background for mentoring the fellow on the knowledge valorisation and innovation dimension of call scope requirement SR-03. The supervisor is not a theorist of commercialisation: he is a practitioner with founded entities in the sensor technology domain. His supervision of the fellow's engagement with demonstrator-oriented work and farmer-facing feedback in WP3 (Field validation, ground truth and uncertainty calibration) and WP2 (Uncertainty-aware decision engine and demonstrator integration) can draw on first-hand experience of the pathway from academic instrument research to commercial product development. This makes the training in knowledge valorisation (one of the SR-03 mandatory dimensions) substantively grounded rather than notional.

His habilitations in both Computer Science and Crop Sciences are the structural guarantee of the fellowship's interdisciplinary coherence from the supervisory side. A supervisor habilitated in Computer Science can guide the probabilistic modelling, Bayesian calibration and data-fusion methodology of WP1 (Probabilistic multi-sensor diagnosis of the field state) and WP2 with specialist technical authority. A supervisor habilitated in Crop Sciences can contextualise those computational methods against the agronomic reality of tomato water stress — the biological reality that the fellow knows from the physiological side — and can evaluate whether the diagnostic outputs from WP1 are agronomically meaningful rather than mathematically elegant but practically vacuous. The combination of both habilitations in a single supervisor is uncommon and is directly aligned with the fellowship's requirement to supervise work that bridges the two domains.

This supervisory profile advances the call's expected outcome EO-05 (enhanced quality and sustainability of research training and supervision) and contributes to expected impact EI-05 (increased alignment with the principles of the European Charter for Researchers), because it provides a supervisory relationship characterised by genuine domain authority on both sides of the disciplinary junction that the fellowship occupies.


2.1.4  The Career Development Plan: the operative instrument of career development

The primary structural measure through which the fellowship's career development is implemented, documented, and monitored is the Career Development Plan (D4-01), a project deliverable of type report delivered by month 3 under WP4 (Training, supervision and two-way transfer of knowledge), with Dr. András Jung as the responsible partner and Dr. Rositsa Cholakova as a contributing partner.

The Career Development Plan is jointly prepared by the supervisor and the fellow, satisfying call scope requirement SR-04, which mandates a Career Development Plan established jointly by supervisor(s) and researcher, covering research objectives, training and career needs including transferable skills, teaching activities, publications and open science activities, and submitted as a project deliverable at the beginning of the action. Submission at month 3 — well before the primary research work of WP1, WP2 and WP3 is substantially advanced — ensures that the career-development framework is prospective rather than retrospective: the competence gaps, training needs, and career targets are documented at the start of the action and used to shape its execution, rather than being reconstructed after the fact.

The career-development significance of the Career Development Plan extends beyond its role as a compliance deliverable. It is the instrument through which:

(a) The fellow's current competences and career trajectory are documented honestly as a starting baseline, establishing the reference point against which development over the 24 months of the fellowship can be measured at each review;

(b) The host-to-fellow and fellow-to-host knowledge-transfer directions are formalised as named, reviewable commitments, creating mutual accountability between supervisor and fellow for the bilateral character of the exchange, not merely for the supervisor's delivery of mentoring;

(c) The training plan across all MSCA-PF mandatory transferable-skills dimensions (addressed in section 2.1.7 below) is documented with specificity and linked to the project's research calendar — so that training in probabilistic machine learning is tied to WP1's timeline, training in knowledge valorisation is tied to WP2's demonstrator development, and so on;

(d) The publication plan, open-science commitments, and conference dissemination strategy are documented in a form that creates accountability over the fellowship timeline, with the Dissemination and exploitation plan (D5-02, month 6) and Data Management Plan (D5-01, month 6) from WP5 (Dissemination, exploitation, communication and management) providing the complementary open-science and data-management frameworks;

(e) The fellow's personal career goals — within academia, outside academia, or spanning both sectors — are made explicit, enabling the supervisor to direct mentoring and network introductions toward the fellow's actual goals rather than toward a generic postdoctoral researcher's generic goals.

The Career Development Plan is reviewed and updated at the interim and final stages of the fellowship. This review cadence is constitutionally important for career development: the plan is not a month-3 filing obligation that becomes stale, but a live document that tracks actual competence development against planned development and adjusts when the research environment shifts. The interim review is timed to coincide with the period following the Diagnostic model specification and calibration report (D1-01, month 14), by which point the fellow's probabilistic modelling competences from WP1 have been substantially advanced through the implementation and calibration tasks T1-01 (Acquire and harmonise multi-sensor EO and meteorological data), T1-02 (Implement Route A direct probabilistic fusion and Route B homogeneous-patch proxy) and T1-03 (Calibrate diagnostic branch and produce field state posterior estimates). The interim review can therefore assess the host-to-fellow computational transfer concretely against actual deliverables, not prospectively against ambitions.

Within WP4, task T4-01 (Prepare, submit and periodically review Career Development Plan) manages the Career Development Plan lifecycle under Dr. András Jung's supervision, while task T4-02 (Deliver structured transferable-skills training and supervision sessions) delivers the structured training programme within which the Career Development Plan's training-needs section is implemented. Eötvös Loránd University (ELTE), Budapest contributes to both tasks as a WP4 contributing partner alongside the supervisor and the fellow.

The Career Development Plan's governance structure satisfies the principles of the European Charter for Researchers — transparent supervision, clear mutual expectations, regular career review, equitable training access — and directly advances the call's expected outcome EO-04 (increased alignment of working conditions for researchers with Charter principles) and expected impact EI-05 (increased alignment with Charter principles, contributing to more equitable and attractive research careers across Europe).


2.1.5  The two-way transfer of knowledge: bilateral career-development significance

The two-way transfer of knowledge structured within WP4 (Training, supervision and two-way transfer of knowledge) is the structural core of the fellowship's career-development model, and its critical feature is that both transfer directions carry substantive career-development weight. Neither direction is a token courtesy contribution by the receiving party; each is independently required by the project's research design.

The host-to-fellow transfer direction delivers the competences that are the fellowship's lasting contribution to Dr. Cholakova's research toolkit. These are competences she does not currently hold at the level required by the project, and they are the competences that will determine the distinctive shape of her post-fellowship career:

— Probabilistic machine learning applied to Earth observation data: the diagnostic branch of WP1 (Probabilistic multi-sensor diagnosis of the field state) requires the fellow to implement and calibrate probabilistic models — including the Bayesian hierarchical models and Gaussian processes referenced in the project's concept note under Route A and Route B — that return full posterior distributions over the latent field state (root-zone soil moisture and crop water status, RQ3) rather than point estimates. This is a substantive step into calibrated probabilistic Earth observation methodology, not an incremental extension of familiar statistical tools. The transition from point-estimate modelling to full-posterior modelling, and from accuracy-percentage validation to calibration-criterion validation (RQ5: 90% prediction-interval coverage), represents a genuine change in the fellow's methodological capability.

— Multi-sensor data fusion across heterogeneous satellite and ground-based sources: WP1 tasks T1-01 and T1-02 require the fellow to work concurrently with Sentinel-1 SAR, Sentinel-2 optical, PlanetScope (access confirmed secured via the Planet platform and API, RQ8), and ERA5 meteorological reanalysis data within a common probabilistic framework. Learning to pre-process, harmonise and model across heterogeneous sensor streams — each with different spatial resolutions, temporal cadences, noise characteristics, and access patterns — is a hands-on data-management and methodological competence that requires supervised practice on real sensor streams. Dr. András Jung's expertise in hyperspectral imaging, field spectroscopy and multisensor-drone fusion, anchored by the Multisensor-Drone-Fusion Working Group (project ELTE TKP2021-NVA-29), makes this transfer practically grounded: the fellow learns from a supervisor with direct technical authority over the methodological domain she is entering.

— Uncertainty-aware crop-model calibration: WP2 (Uncertainty-aware decision engine and demonstrator integration) requires the fellow to execute uncertainty-aware AquaCrop calibration that retains an honest parameter posterior rather than collapsing to a single overconfident parameter set, through task T2-01 (Implement uncertainty-aware AquaCrop calibration and parameter posterior). Propagating that parameter uncertainty through counterfactual irrigation simulations over weather ensembles (T2-02: Develop counterfactual irrigation simulation and WUE-based decision engine) and into a water-use-efficiency-optimised recommendation constitutes a second major host-to-fellow competence transfer: uncertainty-aware crop modelling is a methodological capability that is distinct from standard AquaCrop application and requires both statistical training and supervised implementation.

— Research demonstrator design and development: task T2-03 (Build and integrate research demonstrator web MVP) gives the fellow hands-on experience of building and integrating a software system that exercises the full observation-to-decision pipeline and presents probabilistic recommendations in a form accessible to practitioner audiences. Designing software that communicates uncertainty to non-specialists — the farmer or agronomist, in the context of AgroVIR's iterative feedback — is a competence that bridges research practice and applied deployment.

— Geoinformatics data infrastructure and FAIR EO data management: operating within the Faculty of Informatics at Eötvös Loránd University (ELTE), Budapest gives the fellow direct exposure to geospatial data management, EO data pipeline design, and the research infrastructure required for large-scale multi-sensor data processing. The Data Management Plan (D5-01, month 6), which the fellow leads as responsible partner of WP5 (Dissemination, exploitation, communication and management), formalises the FAIR-compliance framework for the project's heterogeneous data assets and provides a structured context within which data stewardship competences are developed.

The fellow-to-host transfer direction carries a different but equally substantive career-development significance, because it is the mechanism through which the fellowship's career contribution extends beyond the fellow herself to the host institution's capacity:

— Non-destructive physiological measurement protocol design and execution: the validation campaign in WP3 (Field validation, ground truth and uncertainty calibration), led by the fellow through tasks T3-01 (Design and run field validation protocol on Hungarian tomato farms), T3-02 (Assess uncertainty calibration quality against RQ5 target) and T3-03 (Run co-located patch-covariation campaign for Route B validation), is built entirely around non-destructive physiological instrumentation — chlorophyll fluorescence, stomatal conductance, canopy/leaf temperature and spectral reflectance (RQ4) — that represents Dr. Cholakova's core specialist expertise. The ELTE geoinformatics group does not currently hold this competence at the operational level. Through the fellow's design and execution of the field validation protocol, the group acquires capacity in non-destructive agricultural ground-truth measurement that persists in the group's research infrastructure after the fellowship ends, enabling future precision agriculture research that grounds EO estimates against physiological reality.

— Biological interpretation of geoinformatic outputs: the fellow's disciplinary ability to interpret what chlorophyll fluorescence or stomatal conductance actually indicates about a plant's water status, and why a given physiological measurement can or cannot serve as a reliable ground-truth proxy for a satellite-derived spectral index, provides an interpretive layer that the host's geoinformatics group would not otherwise possess. This biological interpretation capacity is relevant not only to the current project but to any future precision agriculture research at ELTE that requires expert assessment of whether EO-derived crop-water-state estimates are agronomically meaningful.

The bilateral accountability for both transfer directions is formally built into the Career Development Plan (D4-01): the CDP review at each reporting milestone requires documented evidence of transfer events in both directions, creating mutual accountability rather than dependence on the supervisor's goodwill. This bilateral documentation structure satisfies the confirmed project outcome OUT-6 (Enhanced researcher competences and career readiness) and the confirmed impact stream IMP-4 (Advancement of the researcher's career and the European Research Area), both grounded in the project's architecture inputs and confirmed for the fellow, host and supervisor identities.


2.1.6  Specific measures enhancing career perspectives within academia

The fellowship implements the following specific measures targeting career development within the academic research sector:

Scientific publication in an identified and defended literature gap. The systematic review of 50 studies on multi-sensor crop water stress monitoring that anchors the project's novelty argument identifies the cell Real-Time Decision Support × PlanetScope as genuinely empty in the reviewed literature (research-gap matrix METH-SOTA-007, referenced in the concept note). A peer-reviewed contribution filling this cell — the project's end-to-end probabilistic fusion-to-decision framework, documented through the Diagnostic model specification and calibration report (D1-01, month 14), the Decision engine and demonstrator software (D2-01, month 20), and the Field validation dataset and uncertainty calibration report (D3-01, month 24) — constitutes a publication portfolio in a niche where the fellow has a distinctive cross-disciplinary voice that pure EO researchers cannot easily replicate and pure physiologists cannot easily claim. Publication in a documented and narrow gap is a more durable academic career contribution than publication in an already crowded field, and the fellow's combined competence profile gives her the standing to claim the novelty credibly on both its scientific dimensions.

All publications arising from the project are committed to open-access routes in compliance with the Horizon Europe open-access mandate, formalised through the Dissemination and exploitation plan (D5-02, month 6) under WP5 (Dissemination, exploitation, communication and management). Open-access publication maximises visibility, citation potential and community uptake, and directly supports the accumulation of a bibliometric record relevant to academic career advancement. The fellow leads WP5 as its responsible partner, giving her direct authorial responsibility for the dissemination framework under task T5-01 (Develop and implement open-science dissemination and communication strategy).

Research leadership experience across four work packages. As the responsible partner leading WP1 (Probabilistic multi-sensor diagnosis of the field state), WP2 (Uncertainty-aware decision engine and demonstrator integration), WP3 (Field validation, ground truth and uncertainty calibration) and WP5 (Dissemination, exploitation, communication and management) — four of the project's five work packages — the fellow accumulates documented research leadership experience that is directly relevant to future applications for senior researcher positions and independent grant funding. Leading the field validation campaign (WP3, tasks T3-01 through T3-03), the probabilistic diagnostic modelling work (WP1, tasks T1-01 through T1-03) and the uncertainty-aware decision engine development (WP2, tasks T2-01 through T2-03) simultaneously gives her a record of managing technically heterogeneous project activities against defined deliverable deadlines and quality criteria. This record provides concrete material for the work-experience sections of future research position applications, fellowship applications and ERC starting-grant applications.

Open benchmark dataset as a standing and citable academic research contribution. The Field validation dataset and uncertainty calibration report (D3-01, month 24), released openly with a persistent identifier (DOI or open repository reference) under FAIR principles as mandated by the Data Management Plan (D5-01, month 6), constitutes a standing contribution to the precision agriculture and EO communities that accumulates citation impact independently of the fellow's ongoing publication record. A curated, publicly released benchmark dataset from Hungarian tomato farms, comprising non-destructive physiological ground-truth measurements paired with matched multi-sensor EO data streams, is a community resource that other researchers in probabilistic multi-sensor crop-water diagnosis can use, validate against, and cite. Dataset citations are increasingly counted alongside paper citations in academic assessment and provide a durable scientific legacy that extends beyond the fellowship period.

Network building within the international geoinformatics, EO and precision agriculture research community. The fellow's residency at Eötvös Loránd University (ELTE), Budapest, under the supervision of Dr. András Jung, integrates her into the international network that Dr. András Jung's research programme in multisensor-drone fusion and hyperspectral imaging has built. Direct participation in the host group's research seminars, collaboration on peer-reviewed outputs, and presence at relevant international conferences (such as ISPRS, IEEE IGARSS and precision agriculture-focused venues referenced in the dissemination approach) builds the fellow's personal research reputation and the professional relationships through which academic career opportunities — collaborations, co-authorships, guest seminar invitations, research position referrals — are generated. This network is complementary to, rather than overlapping with, the fellow's existing Bulgarian plant-physiology network, so the career-development benefit is additive rather than duplicative.

Research integrity and scientific honesty as a practised competence. The project's defining methodological commitment — maintaining an honest uncertainty chain from observation through probabilistic diagnosis through decision, with all outputs satisfying the 90% prediction-interval coverage criterion (RQ5) and pilot success defined as that calibration target being met on the validation set (RQ7) — provides the fellow with a sustained, practised engagement with calibrated scientific honesty that is directly relevant to her reputation and career within a research community that increasingly values reproducible and calibrated results over accuracy metrics alone. A researcher who can design and execute a calibration validation study (the central content of WP3 and D3-01) has a methodological credential that is relevant to the academic communities in probabilistic crop modelling, Bayesian EO estimation, and precision agriculture decision support.


2.1.7  Specific measures enhancing career perspectives outside academia

The fellowship implements the following specific measures targeting career development outside the academic research sector:

Demonstrator-oriented software development for practitioner-facing decision support. Task T2-03 (Build and integrate research demonstrator web MVP) under WP2 (Uncertainty-aware decision engine and demonstrator integration) requires the fellow to design, build and integrate a software tool that exercises the full observation-to-decision pipeline and presents WUE-optimised irrigation recommendations alongside their stated uncertainty in a form accessible to farmer and agronomist audiences. Building a system that communicates probabilistic outputs to non-specialist users — not as statistical distributions but as actionable recommendations with stated confidence ranges — is a software development and science-communication competence that is directly relevant to employment in the agri-tech sector, at precision agriculture technology companies, in agricultural advisory and extension services, and in applied research organisations. The Decision engine and demonstrator software (D2-01, month 20), delivered as open-source software under FAIR principles, constitutes a portfolio artefact that is citable in non-academic applications.

Direct engagement with the non-academic agricultural sector through AgroVIR. The confirmed associated partner AgroVIR (Hungary) provides farmer access and field validation support for WP3, and the fellow's iterative interaction with AgroVIR's farmer network and agronomic advisory context during tasks T3-01 (Design and run field validation protocol on Hungarian tomato farms) gives her first-hand experience of the non-academic translation context: what practitioners need from a probabilistic decision-support tool, how they interact with uncertainty-qualified recommendations, and what institutional factors govern whether a research prototype progresses toward applied deployment. This experience is not simulated or theoretical; it occurs in the real agricultural context of Hungarian tomato farms and with a real commercial associated partner. This direct non-academic sector engagement is a career asset that is relevant to any position at the applied or commercial end of the precision agriculture spectrum, where the ability to translate academic research into practitioner value is a primary selection criterion.

Knowledge valorisation and entrepreneurship training grounded in a supervisor with commercial experience. Call scope requirement SR-03 mandates that training activities include knowledge valorisation and innovation and entrepreneurship. In this fellowship, this dimension is not filled by a generic business-plan writing module but by concrete mentoring from a supervisor — Dr. András Jung, co-founder of Cubert GmbH (hyperspectral cameras) and Brightic Research — who has direct commercial experience of the pathway from academic instrument research to commercial product development. Under his supervision, the fellow learns to articulate the value proposition of a probabilistic decision-support tool for water-use-efficient irrigation, to elicit and incorporate practitioner feedback through AgroVIR's engagement, and to think about the conditions under which a TRL 3–4 research prototype might credibly progress toward TRL 5–7 deployment by a commercial actor or a public extension service. These competences are directly relevant to non-academic career positions in agri-tech firms, agricultural consulting organisations, public extension agencies and research-commercialisation bodies.

FAIR data stewardship and open-source software development as non-academic technical competences. The practical experience of designing and delivering a FAIR-compliant Data Management Plan (D5-01, month 6) for a multi-sensor EO and field-measurement project, and of releasing open-source software (D2-01) and a FAIR-compliant benchmark dataset (D3-01) under permissive licences, constitutes a set of data and software governance competences that are directly relevant to employment in public research data infrastructures, national agriculture data agencies, environmental monitoring organisations, and digital agriculture consultancy firms. These organisations increasingly require researchers who are not only technically capable but operationally fluent in FAIR data practices and open-science governance.


2.1.8  Training across MSCA-PF mandatory transferable-skills dimensions: project-grounded implementation

Call scope requirement SR-03 mandates that training activities integrate key transferable skills and competences common to all fields, including digital ones — explicitly naming generative AI — and foster open science, knowledge valorisation, innovation and entrepreneurship, good scientific conduct and research integrity. In this fellowship, each mandatory dimension is implemented as an integral element of the project's own research content rather than as an appended stand-alone module.
