The Career Development Plan (D4-01), jointly prepared under SR-04 and delivered at month 3, documents the training plan for each dimension with specificity and links each dimension to the project's research calendar through task T4-02 (Deliver structured transferable-skills training and supervision sessions) under WP4 (Training, supervision and two-way transfer of knowledge).

Digital and AI skills, including the responsible use of generative AI. The project's probabilistic machine-learning implementation in WP1 (Probabilistic multi-sensor diagnosis of the field state) — calibrating Bayesian diagnostic models (Bayesian hierarchical models, Gaussian processes) that return full posteriors over root-zone soil moisture and crop water status (RQ3) from heterogeneous multi-sensor inputs — constitutes a sustained, practitioner-level engagement with the state of the art in applied probabilistic AI for environmental sensing. This is not a survey of AI methodology but a hands-on training in design, calibration and validation of probabilistic models on real sensor data streams, under the direct supervision of a researcher with specialist authority in multisensor data fusion. The specifically named sub-competence in SR-03 — responsible use of generative AI — is addressed in the context of environmental modelling and scientific coding, where the project's defining quality standard (honest, calibrated uncertainty: RQ5) creates a natural and rigorous criterion for evaluating any AI-assisted component. A project that defines pilot success as the calibration criterion being met on the validation set (RQ7) — rather than as an arbitrarily selected accuracy metric — is a project whose research culture is precisely calibrated to the responsible use of AI: every tool used, including generative AI assistance, must be assessed against whether it preserves or undermines the honest uncertainty chain from observation to decision.

Knowledge valorisation and innovation and entrepreneurship. The project's demonstrator-oriented output in WP2 (Uncertainty-aware decision engine and demonstrator integration) and the fellowship's partnership with AgroVIR provide the applied context that this SR-03 dimension requires. The fellow learns to position a research prototype for end-user uptake in a concrete agricultural setting, receives practitioner feedback from AgroVIR during WP3, and does so under the mentorship of a supervisor with direct commercial experience in sensor technology commercialisation. The result is a valorisation training that is grounded in actual end-user engagement and actual commercial precedent, not in simulated entrepreneurship exercises.

Research integrity and good scientific conduct. The project's methodological heart — maintaining an honest uncertainty chain from observation to recommendation, with calibrated output meeting the 90% prediction-interval coverage criterion (RQ5) and pilot success defined as that criterion being met on the validation set (RQ7) — provides a natural, sustained and substantive training context for research integrity. A researcher who designs and executes a calibration validation study in WP3 learns, through the doing, the difference between a model that is accurate in expectation and one that reports its own uncertainty honestly; between optimistic claims and calibrated claims; and between validation that tests whether reported uncertainty is trustworthy and validation that only tests whether predictions are close to observed values on average. These are research-integrity competences of substantive scientific value, acquired through practice rather than through a declared commitment to integrity principles.

Open science and FAIR data stewardship. The Data Management Plan (D5-01, month 6) and the Dissemination and exploitation plan (D5-02, month 6) — both led by the fellow as responsible partner of WP5 (Dissemination, exploitation, communication and management) — constitute the operative open-science training framework. Writing and maintaining a FAIR-compliant Data Management Plan for a multi-sensor EO project that generates heterogeneous data types — satellite imagery from Sentinel-1 SAR, Sentinel-2 optical and PlanetScope; meteorological reanalysis from ERA5; non-destructive physiological field measurements (chlorophyll fluorescence, stomatal conductance, canopy/leaf temperature, spectral reflectance); crop model calibration outputs and uncertainty records — is a substantive FAIR data stewardship exercise that requires active engagement with findability, accessibility, interoperability and reusability across research data types that differ fundamentally in format, provenance and licensing. The open-source release of the Diagnostic model specification and calibration report (D1-01), the Decision engine and demonstrator software (D2-01) and the Field validation dataset and uncertainty calibration report (D3-01) under FAIR principles provides practical experience of end-to-end open science practice that is directly transferable to any future research position operating under national or European open-data mandates.


2.1.9  Expected contribution of skills development to the future career of the researcher

The expected career contribution of the fellowship's skills-development programme is assessed at the level of the structural career outcome it creates, rather than at the level of specific numeric targets, for a reason that is both principled and transparent: specific quantitative targets — publication counts, training hours, thesis co-supervision figures, seminar counts and follow-on proposal deadlines — are not operator-provided and are therefore not asserted here. They are to be fixed in the Career Development Plan (D4-01) jointly by Dr. András Jung and Dr. Rositsa Cholakova at the start of the action and updated at each review point in conformance with SR-04. What can be asserted with rigour is the structure of the career contribution and the reasons why that structure is distinctive and durable.

The structural outcome of the fellowship's skills-development programme is the consolidation of a cross-disciplinary competence profile that couples:

— plant physiology and non-destructive stress phenotyping in tomato horticulture, based on approximately four years of post-doctoral specialist practice including a summa cum laude doctoral thesis on the non-destructive evaluation of the physiological status of drought-stressed tomato plants (doi:10.2139/ssrn.5492527) and further published work on stress physiology and biostimulants;

— probabilistic machine learning, Bayesian multi-sensor calibration and uncertainty quantification acquired through the implementation and calibration tasks of WP1 (Probabilistic multi-sensor diagnosis of the field state);

— multi-sensor Earth observation data fusion using Sentinel-1 SAR, Sentinel-2 optical, PlanetScope (confirmed secured) and ERA5 meteorological reanalysis, acquired through tasks T1-01 and T1-02 of WP1;

— uncertainty-aware crop-model calibration through the AquaCrop parameter-posterior framework of WP2 (Uncertainty-aware decision engine and demonstrator integration), implemented in task T2-01;

— field-scale validation protocol design, execution and calibration assessment under non-destructive physiological ground-truth measurement, developed and executed through WP3 (Field validation, ground truth and uncertainty calibration) tasks T3-01 through T3-03;

— FAIR data management, open-source software development and academic dissemination strategy, executed through WP5 (Dissemination, exploitation, communication and management) and the Data Management Plan (D5-01) and Dissemination and exploitation plan (D5-02).

This specific combination is the fellowship's lasting contribution to Dr. Cholakova's career. Its distinctiveness derives from the fact that the plant-physiology and the probabilistic EO halves of the profile are mutually reinforcing rather than merely additive: each half makes the other more valuable, because the quality of a probabilistic crop-water-state estimate is ultimately judged against physiological ground truth, and the value of a physiological measurement campaign is amplified when it can be connected to a scalable satellite-based probabilistic monitoring framework. A researcher who holds both is positioned differently from a researcher who holds either one alone.

Within academia, the profile positions Dr. Rositsa Cholakova for research leadership in precision agriculture or Earth observation at an institution requiring cross-disciplinary capacity in agri-environmental sensing. The peer-reviewed publication portfolio from the fellowship — contributions to probabilistic multi-sensor crop-water diagnosis, uncertainty-aware irrigation decision support, and calibration methodology — addresses a documented literature gap and provides a citation record that is directly relevant to academic career advancement. The research leadership experience from leading WP1 through WP3 and WP5 provides the project management record that grant agencies assess in principal investigator evaluations. The open benchmark dataset (D3-01, FAIR release with DOI) provides a standing community contribution that accumulates citations independently of ongoing publications.

Outside academia, the profile is directly relevant to agri-tech companies developing precision irrigation decision-support systems; to agricultural advisory and extension services translating probabilistic EO methods for practitioner audiences; to environmental consulting organisations using crop-water modelling for water-resource planning; and to agricultural research organisations — including, potentially, the Bulgarian Agricultural Academy, the fellow's current institutional home — that are developing data-driven precision agriculture capacities. The demonstrator experience (WP2, D2-01) and the AgroVIR engagement (WP3) provide first-hand non-academic sector experience that is directly citable in non-academic career applications.

At the level of call expected impacts, the career-development measures described in this sub-section realise the confirmed project impact stream IMP-4 (Advancement of the researcher's career and the European Research Area). They map directly to expected impact EI-01 (improved employability and career prospects of MSCA postdoctoral fellows within academia and beyond, contributing to a more mobile and highly skilled European research workforce), to expected impact EI-05 (increased alignment of working conditions for researchers with the principles of the European Charter for Researchers, contributing to more equitable and attractive research careers across Europe), and to expected impact EI-07 (new mind-sets and approaches to R&I work fostered through international, inter-sectoral and interdisciplinary experience, enriching the broader European research culture). The confirmed call expected outcomes addressed are EO-01 (increased set of research and transferable skills and competences, leading to improved employability and career prospects), EO-02 (new mind-sets and approaches to R&I work forged through international and interdisciplinary experience), EO-04 (increased alignment of working conditions for researchers with Charter principles) and EO-05 (enhanced quality and sustainability of research training and supervision).

sub_sections.title: Suitability and quality of the measures to maximise expected outcomes and impacts, as set out in the dissemination and exploitation plan, including communication activities
sub_sections.content:
2.2  Suitability and quality of the measures to maximise expected outcomes and impacts, as set out in the dissemination and exploitation plan, including communication activities

This sub-section addresses the second Impact sub-criterion: whether the project's dissemination, exploitation, and communication measures are well-designed, adequately targeted, proportionate to the project's scale, and credibly linked to concrete actions that will realise the call's expected outcomes and impacts during and after the 24-month fellowship. The account is organised in nine parts: (i) the rationale and structural logic of the dissemination, exploitation and communication approach; (ii) the two foundational framework deliverables that govern the approach prospectively; (iii) scientific dissemination — target research communities, open-access publication strategy, and conference channels; (iv) open-source code and FAIR benchmark dataset release as the primary exploitation and community-building mechanism; (v) communication to practitioner and non-specialist audiences via the associated partner AgroVIR; (vi) the research-to-teaching feedback loop through curriculum integration at Eötvös Loránd University (ELTE), Budapest; (vii) exploitation through institutional research capacity building at ELTE as a post-project durable outcome; (viii) the intellectual property rights strategy and its grounding in the project's TRL scope and MSCA instrument logic; and (ix) the proportionality of the measures to the 24-month European Fellowship scale and their consolidated mapping to call expected outcomes and impacts.


2.2.1  Rationale and structural logic of the dissemination, exploitation and communication approach

The project's dissemination, exploitation and communication approach is not a generic open-science appendix. It is calibrated to three specific characteristics of this project that jointly determine the form and ambition of the approach: the project's TRL scope, the nature of its primary outputs, and the structure of its target communities.

The TRL scope — a research prototype at TRL 3–4 (RQ10, operator-confirmed) over a 24-month European Fellowship — sets the appropriate level of exploitation ambition. The project does not produce an operational commercial product, does not achieve field-scale deployment, and does not assert quantified water savings at scale. Its impact is realised through scientific knowledge production, open-infrastructure creation, and institutional capacity building, not through direct market uptake. The dissemination, exploitation and communication strategy is calibrated accordingly: it targets scientific peers, developers of subsequent systems, and the educational community, while using the practitioner engagement with AgroVIR to ground the research prototype in real-world agricultural context — without misrepresenting the TRL-appropriate engagement as operational deployment.

The nature of the primary outputs — three research deliverables across the technical work packages, two framework deliverables governing open science, and one career development deliverable — creates a specific dissemination timeline. The Diagnostic model specification and calibration report (D1-01, month 14) from WP1 (Probabilistic multi-sensor diagnosis of the field state) is the first major scientific output; the Decision engine and demonstrator software (D2-01, month 20) from WP2 (Uncertainty-aware decision engine and demonstrator integration) is the second; and the Field validation dataset and uncertainty calibration report (D3-01, month 24) from WP3 (Field validation, ground truth and uncertainty calibration) is the final and closing scientific output. Each output is scientifically distinct and addresses a different dimension of the project's novelty claim — probabilistic multi-sensor fusion, uncertainty-aware crop-model-based decision support, and calibration validation — so the dissemination strategy is naturally phased across the fellowship timeline rather than concentrated at the end.

The structure of the target communities is dual: a scientific community comprising multi-sensor Earth observation, Bayesian probabilistic modelling, crop-water-state estimation, and precision agriculture decision-support researchers; and a practitioner community comprising tomato horticulturalists and their agronomic advisors, reachable through the associated partner AgroVIR (Hungary). These two communities require different communication registers, different dissemination channels, and different output formats. The dissemination, exploitation and communication strategy addresses both without conflating them.

The operative instruments through which the approach is established and maintained are WP5 (Dissemination, exploitation, communication and management), led by Dr. Rositsa Cholakova as responsible partner, with Eötvös Loránd University (ELTE), Budapest contributing. Task T5-01 (Develop and implement open-science dissemination and communication strategy) and task T5-02 (Manage project coordination, reporting and ethics oversight) are the two work-package-level mechanisms. Two deliverables frame the approach prospectively: the Data Management Plan (D5-01, month 6) and the Dissemination and exploitation plan (D5-02, month 6). Their joint delivery at month 6 — before any primary research output is produced from WP1, WP2 or WP3 — ensures that the FAIR data stewardship and dissemination commitments are established as prospective obligations rather than retrospectively applied policies.


2.2.2  The two foundational framework deliverables: Data Management Plan and Dissemination and exploitation plan

The Data Management Plan (D5-01, month 6) and the Dissemination and exploitation plan (D5-02, month 6) are the structural foundation of the project's dissemination and exploitation strategy. Each serves a distinct and non-redundant function, and their combined early delivery is the architectural guarantee that the project's open-science commitments are designed in advance of the outputs they govern.

The Data Management Plan (D5-01) establishes FAIR compliance — findable, accessible, interoperable, reusable — as the governing standard for all primary project data assets and software outputs. The data assets it must cover are heterogeneous: multi-sensor Earth observation imagery from Sentinel-1 SAR, Sentinel-2 optical, and PlanetScope (access confirmed via the Planet platform and API, RQ8); meteorological reanalysis from ERA5; non-destructive physiological field measurements collected in WP3 (chlorophyll fluorescence, stomatal conductance, canopy/leaf temperature and spectral reflectance, RQ4) from Hungarian tomato farm sites accessed via AgroVIR; uncertainty-aware AquaCrop calibration outputs and counterfactual simulation records produced in WP2; and probabilistic posterior estimates from the diagnostic branch of WP1. These data types differ fundamentally in format (raster imagery, time-series tabular measurements, model calibration posteriors), provenance (open Copernicus data, commercial PlanetScope, field-collected physiological data, model-derived outputs), licensing (open licence, confirmed-secured commercial, project-generated), and reusability constraints. A DMP that addresses them uniformly rather than individually would be formally compliant but practically insufficient; the D5-01 DMP is designed to address each category of data asset with the specificity required to operationalise FAIR principles for it.

The Horizon Europe open-access mandate applies unconditionally to all peer-reviewed publications arising from the project. The Data Management Plan (D5-01) records this commitment formally for project-generated publications alongside the data commitments. The combination of open-access publication and FAIR-compliant data release operationalises the call's expected impact EI-02 (increased and broadened R&I impact through enhanced networking and communication) by ensuring that all scientific outputs from the project reach the widest possible audience without access barriers.

The KPI-03 verifiable indicator for D5-01 is: submission by month 6 with coverage of all WP1, WP2 and WP3 data assets confirmed under FAIR principles. The KPI-11 verifiable indicator additionally checks that FAIR compliance is confirmed for the full range of primary research outputs including WP1 through WP3. Together these two KPIs make D5-01 not a one-time filing obligation but an auditable commitment that can be checked at each project reporting milestone.

The Dissemination and exploitation plan (D5-02) performs a complementary function: it identifies open-access dissemination routes for all primary research outputs of WP1, WP2 and WP3, and documents the communication strategy to both scientific and non-specialist audiences. It specifies international venues for peer-reviewed publication (at minimum covering WP1 and WP2 primary results), open repository routes for open data and code releases, and the communication approach to practitioner and farmer audiences via AgroVIR. D5-02 is an active document: it is updated periodically as WP1 through WP3 outputs materialise across the fellowship timeline, so that the dissemination commitments remain current rather than reflecting only the month-6 expectations of outputs that may evolve. This periodic update structure is the guarantee that D5-02 is a living dissemination management tool rather than a boilerplate plan filed once and forgotten.

The KPI-04 verifiable indicator for D5-02 is: submission by month 6 with open-access routes confirmed for all primary research outputs of WP1, WP2 and WP3. The KPI-07 verifiable indicator additionally checks that international open-access venues are identified specifically for the WP1 and WP2 outputs, reflecting the specific community-positioning strategy for those outputs (addressing the real-time decision-support × PlanetScope gap, METH-SOTA-007) rather than generic open-access compliance.

Taken together, the early delivery of D5-01 and D5-02 at month 6 means that by the time the first substantive research output (D1-01, month 14) is produced, the entire open-science framework is already in place and operative. There is no risk that a significant research result will be produced without a Data Management Plan, or disseminated without a strategy for doing so, or released without FAIR compliance established for its data category. This prospective design is the strongest possible structural guarantee against the common failure mode of dissemination planning being bolted on retroactively at the end of a project.


2.2.3  Scientific dissemination: target communities, open-access publication strategy, and conference channels

The primary scientific dissemination route is open-access peer-reviewed publication. The project's three technical work packages each produce distinct scientific contributions that are independently publishable and target identifiable bodies of literature.

WP1 (Probabilistic multi-sensor diagnosis of the field state), culminating in the Diagnostic model specification and calibration report (D1-01, month 14), produces the central methodological contribution: the end-to-end probabilistic fusion framework coupling Route A direct multi-sensor probabilistic fusion (Sentinel-1 SAR, Sentinel-2 optical, PlanetScope and ERA5 meteorological reanalysis fused into a calibrated posterior over root-zone soil moisture and crop water status, RQ3) and Route B homogeneous patch proxy architecture (sidestepping the sub-pixel resolution problem by reading a spectrally and biologically homogeneous proxy patch that covaries with the target tomato crop, RQ2). The defended scientific novelty of this contribution — the end-to-end coupling of learned multimodal fusion, explicit probabilistic crop-water-state estimation outputs, and water-use-efficiency-oriented decision optimisation, argued narrowly against acknowledged Bayesian precedents in the literature — positions it in the multi-sensor Earth observation, probabilistic crop-water modelling and remote sensing precision agriculture literatures. The target publication community includes researchers in Bayesian multi-sensor fusion, hyperspectral and satellite-based crop-water-state estimation, and calibration methodology. International conference dissemination is targeted at ISPRS and IEEE IGARSS venues, which are the canonical international conferences for this research community, as well as precision agriculture conference venues addressing the real-time decision-support × PlanetScope gap identified in the research-gap matrix (METH-SOTA-007). Conference presentations from WP1 are expected from month 14 onwards, following D1-01 delivery.

WP2 (Uncertainty-aware decision engine and demonstrator integration), culminating in the Decision engine and demonstrator software (D2-01, month 20), produces a second distinct scientific contribution: the uncertainty-aware AquaCrop calibration retaining an honest parameter posterior rather than collapsing to a single overconfident parameter set, combined with counterfactual irrigation simulations over weather ensembles and a water-use-efficiency-based decision objective (RQ6). The scientific community targeted by this contribution is that of uncertainty-aware crop modelling and precision irrigation decision support — a community that spans agronomy, crop physiology, hydrological modelling and decision science, and that has distinct publication venues from the EO fusion community targeted by WP1. The decision to use WUE (water-use efficiency) as the decision objective (RQ6, operator-confirmed) rather than yield maximisation or profit is itself a scientific statement about the appropriate objective function for water-constrained irrigation decision support that is worth articulating in the scientific literature and defending against alternative formulations. The target publication timing for WP2-derived contributions runs from month 20 through the end of the fellowship, with conference presentation possible from month 14 if WP2 work in progress is sufficiently advanced.

WP3 (Field validation, ground truth and uncertainty calibration), culminating in the Field validation dataset and uncertainty calibration report (D3-01, month 24), produces a third scientific contribution of a different character: a calibration study. The scientific question addressed by the WP3 output is not 'how accurate is the model?' but 'are the model's stated uncertainty bounds honest?' — measured by the 90% prediction-interval coverage criterion (RQ5: 90% prediction intervals containing the ground truth approximately 90% of the time on the validation set). This calibration framing is a scientific contribution in its own right in the literature on probabilistic forecasting validation, where calibration is increasingly recognised as distinct from and more informative than accuracy for probabilistic model assessment. The WP3 publication also presents the non-destructive physiological ground-truth measurement protocol for tomato water stress under Hungarian farm conditions — chlorophyll fluorescence, stomatal conductance, canopy/leaf temperature and spectral reflectance (RQ4) — which is a contribution to the precision agriculture instrumentation and validation literature that is valuable independently of the EO modelling context. The target publication venues for WP3-derived contributions therefore span the calibration-methodology, probabilistic forecasting, and precision agriculture experimental communities.

All peer-reviewed publications arising from WP1, WP2 and WP3 are committed to open-access routes in compliance with the Horizon Europe open-access mandate, confirmed through the Dissemination and exploitation plan (D5-02, month 6) and the Data Management Plan (D5-01, month 6). The fellow leads both D5-01 and D5-02 as responsible partner of WP5, giving her direct authorial responsibility for the open-access framework under task T5-01 (Develop and implement open-science dissemination and communication strategy). This responsibility is not delegated to Eötvös Loránd University (ELTE), Budapest as the host institution; it is owned by the fellow, which reflects the MSCA-PF principle that the fellowship's scientific output is the fellow's primary career contribution and that the fellow takes active responsibility for its dissemination.

The scientific dissemination approach directly realises the call's expected outcome EO-03 (enhanced networking and communication capacities with scientific peers) and expected impact EI-02 (increased and broadened R&I impact through enhanced networking and communication). It also realises EI-04 (increased global attractiveness, visibility and reputation of the participating organisation and the ERA) by positioning Eötvös Loránd University (ELTE), Budapest as the home of innovative open research in multi-sensor probabilistic crop-water diagnosis — filling a documented literature gap and making the evidence freely available to the international precision agriculture and Earth observation research community.


2.2.4  Open-source code and FAIR benchmark dataset release as the primary exploitation and community-building mechanism

The project's open-source software and benchmark dataset releases constitute its primary exploitation mechanism at TRL 3–4. The case for this primacy is grounded in a specific community need: few openly available end-to-end implementations currently link multi-sensor Earth observation, probabilistic crop-water-state estimation and irrigation decision optimisation in a reproducible, FAIR-compliant package. The releases from this project address that gap directly and in a form that the research community can use, extend and build upon without requiring access to the project team.

Three releases are planned, timed to the delivery of the three technical deliverables:

First release, month 14 (accompanying D1-01): the open-source code repository for the probabilistic multi-sensor diagnostic model produced by WP1. This repository covers the Route A direct probabilistic fusion implementation and the Route B homogeneous patch proxy implementation, together with the calibration framework and all pre-processing code for harmonising Sentinel-1 SAR, Sentinel-2 optical, PlanetScope and ERA5 meteorological reanalysis inputs. The code is released under a permissive open-source licence specified in the Data Management Plan (D5-01). FAIR compliance for this release is confirmed by D5-01 at month 6 and operationalised by the open repository at D1-01 delivery (KPI-10: open code repository established alongside D1-01 delivery, FAIR compliance confirmed by DMP).

Second release, month 20 (accompanying D2-01): the Decision engine and demonstrator software — an openly licensed, replicable end-to-end decision-support prototype at TRL 3–4, as specified in the project's confirmed TRL target (RQ10). This release covers the uncertainty-aware AquaCrop calibration implementation producing an honest parameter posterior (T2-01: Implement uncertainty-aware AquaCrop calibration and parameter posterior), the counterfactual irrigation simulation over weather ensembles (T2-02: Develop counterfactual irrigation simulation and WUE-based decision engine), and the research demonstrator web MVP (T2-03: Build and integrate research demonstrator web MVP) that exercises the full observation-to-decision pipeline and presents WUE-optimised irrigation recommendations alongside their stated uncertainty. The end-to-end nature of this software release — from multi-sensor EO input through probabilistic crop-water-state diagnosis through uncertainty-aware crop model calibration through WUE-scored counterfactual decision — is the primary value of the release for the community: it provides a reproducible reference implementation that subsequent researchers and developers can fork, adapt and extend, rather than requiring them to reconstruct the entire pipeline from scratch. The KPI-06 verifiable indicator is: D2-01 delivered by month 20 as open-source software with documented WUE-based decision logic.

Third release, month 24 (accompanying D3-01): the open FAIR release of the Field validation dataset and uncertainty calibration report. This release covers the non-destructive physiological ground-truth measurement data from Hungarian tomato farms accessed via AgroVIR — chlorophyll fluorescence, stomatal conductance, canopy/leaf temperature and spectral reflectance (RQ4) measured at co-located field sites across the growing season — together with the matched multi-sensor EO data streams (Sentinel-1, Sentinel-2, PlanetScope, ERA5) and the calibration assessment results against the RQ5 uncertainty-calibration criterion. The dataset is assigned a persistent identifier (DOI or open repository reference) and released under FAIR principles, confirmed by D5-01 (KPI-08: D3-01 released under FAIR principles by month 24 with dataset DOI or open repository reference). This benchmark dataset constitutes an internationally reproducible resource for the probabilistic multi-sensor crop-water diagnosis community: it provides paired physiological and EO data from a real-world tomato horticultural context that can be used by other researchers to validate their own probabilistic sensing methods, calibrate their own models, or train their own probabilistic fusion architectures. Its community value accumulates independently of the fellow's ongoing publication record, because dataset citations are a standing contribution that other researchers accrue over time as they use and extend the resource.

The open-source and benchmark-dataset releases together realise the call's expected impact EI-03 (stronger R&I capacity and output among participating organisations and better transfer of knowledge) by creating open infrastructure that strengthens the global precision agriculture and Earth observation research community, not only Eötvös Loránd University (ELTE), Budapest. They also realise EI-04 (increased global attractiveness, visibility and reputation) by making the project's results internationally findable, accessible and reusable — qualities that attract citations, collaborations and follow-on funding for ELTE and for the fellow beyond the fellowship period.


2.2.5  Communication to practitioner and non-specialist audiences: AgroVIR and farmer engagement

The project's communication to non-specialist audiences is channelled through the confirmed associated partner AgroVIR (Hungary), whose scope is farmer access, field validation support and iterative feedback. AgroVIR's confirmed scope is deliberately bounded: AgroVIR does not own or operate the demonstrator tool, does not carry responsibility for dissemination outputs, and does not carry responsibility for the scientific research programme. Its specific contribution is to provide the project with access to Hungarian tomato farm sites for the WP3 field validation campaign and to provide iterative feedback on the demonstrator's outputs from farmer and agronomic advisory perspectives. This scoping is important for maintaining the TRL-3–4 framing of the project: AgroVIR's engagement is a research grounding mechanism, not a deployment pathway.

The communication value of AgroVIR's engagement operates through two channels. The first is the iterative demonstrator feedback loop. Task T3-01 (Design and run field validation protocol on Hungarian tomato farms) requires the fellow to interact with the farm contexts that AgroVIR provides access to, collecting non-destructive physiological ground truth (chlorophyll fluorescence, stomatal conductance, canopy/leaf temperature and spectral reflectance, RQ4) while also observing the practical farming context in which the demonstrator's outputs would eventually need to be interpretable. The demonstrator's presentation of WUE-optimised irrigation recommendations alongside stated uncertainty ranges — produced by task T2-03 (Build and integrate research demonstrator web MVP) — is informed by iterative feedback from AgroVIR's farming and agronomic advisory network during WP3. The result is a research demonstrator whose uncertainty communication design has been shaped by practitioner perspectives, even at TRL 3–4, rather than being designed purely from a statistical or software engineering standpoint.

The second channel is the potential for the demonstrator to serve as a communication artefact in its own right for farmer audiences. The project's observable output — an irrigation recommendation with a stated confidence range — is comprehensible to a grower audience in a way that a Bayesian posterior distribution over root-zone soil moisture is not. Communication materials addressed to farmer and agronomic advisor audiences can be built around the recommendation layer rather than the probabilistic machinery, and the Dissemination and exploitation plan (D5-02, month 6) provides the framework for developing and recording these materials. The non-specialist communication strategy documented in D5-02 is therefore not a generic press-release commitment but a practitioner-grounded communication approach anchored in the specific output register of WUE-optimised recommendations from a tomato irrigation decision-support context.

The AgroVIR engagement also contributes to the project's role in realising the call's expected impact EI-02 (increased and broadened R&I impact through enhanced networking and communication capacities with scientific peers and the general public). While AgroVIR's primary contribution is to the validation and feedback dimensions of the project, the relationship creates a communication bridge between the project's scientific outputs and the agricultural practitioner community that would not otherwise exist in a purely academic host environment. This bridge is proportionate to the 24-month fellowship scale and the TRL 3–4 scope: it establishes the relationship and the communication channel without asserting operational deployment or quantified practitioner uptake.


2.2.6  Research-to-teaching feedback loop: curriculum integration at Eötvös Loránd University (ELTE), Budapest

Eötvös Loránd University (ELTE), Budapest is a university host with active geoinformatics, remote sensing and precision agriculture teaching curricula at MSc and PhD level within the Faculty of Informatics. This creates a specific dissemination and exploitation route that is structurally guaranteed by the host institution type: the project's research outputs can be incorporated directly into ELTE's teaching, closing the loop between research production and knowledge transmission to the next generation of geoinformatics and precision agriculture researchers and practitioners.

The mechanism operates through two complementary channels. The first is the open-source code release accompanying the Diagnostic model specification and calibration report (D1-01, month 14). The probabilistic multi-sensor diagnostic model and its calibration framework — covering Route A direct probabilistic fusion and Route B homogeneous patch proxy for crop-water-state estimation — are concrete, executable, FAIR-compliant software artefacts that can be incorporated into ELTE's teaching as laboratory exercises, case studies or reproducible workflows for geoinformatics and remote sensing courses. Students can run the code on real Sentinel-1, Sentinel-2 and ERA5 inputs, explore the probabilistic outputs, and understand the calibration criterion (RQ5: 90% prediction-interval coverage) through hands-on engagement with working implementations. This is the kind of pedagogically effective teaching material — worked and verified implementations of state-of-the-art methods — that is often unavailable in publicly accessible form and that universities must otherwise develop internally at significant cost.

The second channel is the open-source decision engine and demonstrator software (D2-01, month 20). The uncertainty-aware AquaCrop calibration and counterfactual irrigation simulation implemented in D2-01 are topics at the current frontier of precision agriculture decision support, and the end-to-end demonstrator exercises the full pipeline from satellite observation to irrigation recommendation in a single, reproducible implementation. At ELTE's MSc and PhD level, this kind of end-to-end working system provides a foundation for advanced courses in uncertainty-aware crop modelling, precision irrigation decision support, and machine learning for agricultural applications — topics that map directly onto the host group's research programme in geoinformatics and multisensor-drone fusion.

Curriculum integration is envisaged from month 18 onwards, following D1-01 delivery at month 14 and in the final phase of D2-01 development at month 20. The FAIR compliance of both releases, confirmed by the Data Management Plan (D5-01, month 6), ensures that the materials can be accessed, reproduced and adapted by ELTE's teaching faculty and students without licensing barriers. This curriculum integration pathway directly realises the call's expected outcome EO-08 (regular feedback of research results into teaching and education at participating organisations) and the call's expected impact EI-06 (regular feedback of research results into teaching and education at participating organisations, sustaining knowledge circulation between research and education). The KPI-10 and KPI-11 verifiable indicators together confirm both channels: KPI-10 requires the open code repository established at D1-01 delivery with FAIR compliance confirmed by D5-01; KPI-11 requires D5-01 by month 6 covering all WP1–WP3 data assets under FAIR principles.

The curriculum integration route is proportionate to the 24-month European Fellowship scale precisely because it requires no additional investment beyond the open-science deliverables that the project is already committed to producing. The open-source releases under FAIR principles are required outputs of the project regardless of curriculum integration; their uptake into ELTE's teaching is an additional impact that flows from the open design without requiring separate effort or resources. This is the mark of a well-designed exploitation route: it realises an additional impact stream from outputs that are already committed, rather than requiring dedicated resources that compete with the research programme's timeline.


2.2.7  Exploitation through institutional research capacity building at Eötvös Loránd University (ELTE), Budapest

The project's primary exploitation outcome at the institutional level is the strengthening of Eötvös Loránd University (ELTE), Budapest's research capacity in probabilistic multi-sensor Earth observation, Bayesian crop-water-state estimation and uncertainty-aware decision support. This capacity-building is not an asserted intention but a structural consequence of the project's deliverable design and knowledge-transfer architecture.

Through WP1 (Probabilistic multi-sensor diagnosis of the field state) and WP2 (Uncertainty-aware decision engine and demonstrator integration), ELTE's geoinformatics and remote sensing research group acquires a documented, validated, openly available methodology for probabilistic multi-sensor crop-water-state estimation and a working implementation of uncertainty-aware irrigation decision support. These outputs persist within ELTE's research infrastructure after the fellowship ends: as open-source code that ELTE researchers and students can use and extend in follow-on projects; as a calibrated probabilistic modelling approach that ELTE's participation in future EO research projects can build on; and as a benchmark validation dataset (D3-01) that other researchers within and outside ELTE can use to test and compare new methods. The open-source code and FAIR dataset releases are therefore simultaneously dissemination outputs and institutional research infrastructure investments.

Through WP3 (Field validation, ground truth and uncertainty calibration) and the fellow-to-host knowledge transfer direction formalised in WP4 (Training, supervision and two-way transfer of knowledge), ELTE's geoinformatics group additionally acquires validated capacity in non-destructive physiological ground-truth measurement for agricultural sensing applications. The validation protocol designed and executed by the fellow through tasks T3-01 (Design and run field validation protocol on Hungarian tomato farms), T3-02 (Assess uncertainty calibration quality against RQ5 target) and T3-03 (Run co-located patch-covariation campaign for Route B validation) represents a specialist capability in agricultural field measurement that the geoinformatics group does not currently hold at the operational level. The fellow-to-host transfer of this capability, documented in the Career Development Plan (D4-01) and evidenced at each periodic review through KPI-02, is the project's contribution to ELTE's research capacity in the precision agriculture experimental domain.

The integration of these outputs into ELTE's ongoing remote sensing and geoinformatics research programme beyond the fellowship period — identified in the Phase 5 impact architecture as exploitation activity with expected result of 'strengthened R&I capacity at ELTE in Bayesian multi-sensor analysis and uncertainty-aware crop-water-state estimation, enabling follow-on research projects building on the project's open-source code and validated methodology' — is the post-project sustainability mechanism through which the fellowship's impact on EI-03 (stronger R&I capacity and output among participating organisations and better transfer of knowledge between participating organisations) extends beyond the 24-month duration. It is realised by design rather than by contingency: the open-science framework (D5-01, D5-02) and the code and data releases (D1-01, D2-01, D3-01) ensure that the research infrastructure remains live and accessible after the project ends, regardless of the fellow's subsequent institutional location.


2.2.8  Intellectual property rights strategy: open science over exclusivity at TRL 3–4

The project's intellectual property rights strategy is explicitly and deliberately non-exclusive. No patent protection is sought. The project's primary outputs — scientific publications, the Diagnostic model specification and calibration report (D1-01), the Decision engine and demonstrator software (D2-01) and the Field validation dataset and uncertainty calibration report (D3-01) — are research artefacts intended for open dissemination under FAIR principles and permissive open-source licences as specified in the Data Management Plan (D5-01, month 6).

The rationale for this IPR posture is grounded in the project's confirmed TRL target (TRL 3–4, RQ10) and the MSCA-PF instrument's knowledge-transfer orientation. At TRL 3–4 — research prototype stage, with the primary scientific questions still concerning whether the probabilistic uncertainty chain can be maintained honestly from observation to decision and whether the calibration criterion (RQ5: 90% prediction-interval coverage) can be met on the validation set (pilot success criterion RQ7) — the impact-maximising strategy is open scientific dissemination and community capacity building, not commercial exclusivity. Patent protection would require a clearly defined and novel technical implementation of sufficient industrial maturity that it could sustain patent examination; at TRL 3–4, the project's output does not meet this standard, and asserting patent protection on a research prototype would delay open scientific dissemination without providing commercially actionable exclusivity. More fundamentally, the fellowship's knowledge-transfer and ERA-capacity objectives (EI-03, EI-04) are advanced by open dissemination and undermined by exclusivity: the value of the project's open-source decision engine to the global precision agriculture research community arises precisely from its being openly available, not from being withheld for commercial licensing.

The permissive open-source licensing approach for D2-01 (Decision engine and demonstrator software) is consistent with the Phase 5 exploitation plan's confirmed IPR strategy: the software is 'intended for open dissemination under FAIR principles and permissive open-source licences' with 'no patent protection sought.' The specific licence terms are to be documented in D5-01 (Data Management Plan) and applied at D2-01 delivery. The permissive-licence choice — as opposed to copyleft — is appropriate for a research prototype intended to be adapted and extended by other researchers and by downstream commercial developers: it maximises community uptake without creating licence-compatibility barriers for integrators.

IP arrangements that might arise from post-fellowship exploitation activity — for example, if a commercial actor or public extension service were to develop the TRL 3–4 prototype into an operational system beyond the fellowship period — are not determined by this proposal and are left to post-project negotiation between the relevant parties, including Eötvös Loránd University (ELTE), Budapest as host institution. The project's open-source releases do not preclude such downstream exploitation; they provide the open foundation on which it could be built, with the licensing terms set to enable rather than obstruct derivative development. This is the appropriate division of responsibility between a research fellowship producing foundational open infrastructure and the subsequent commercial or institutional actors who might deploy it operationally.

The open IPR posture directly supports the call's expected impacts EI-03 (stronger R&I capacity and output, better knowledge transfer) and EI-04 (increased global attractiveness and reputation of ELTE and the ERA): both impacts are realised more effectively through open access than through exclusivity at TRL 3–4. It also supports expected outcome EO-07 (stronger R&I capacity and output among participating organisations; better transfer of knowledge) by ensuring that the knowledge produced by the project flows freely to the scientific and practitioner communities that need it.


2.2.9  Proportionality of measures to the 24-month European Fellowship scale and consolidated mapping to call expected outcomes and impacts

The project's dissemination, exploitation and communication measures are calibrated to the 24-month European Fellowship timeline and the TRL 3–4 research-prototype scope. Proportionality is not a statement about modesty of ambition; it is a statement about realism in the claimed output-to-impact chain. A dissemination plan that claimed operational deployment of a commercial irrigation decision-support system from a 24-month academic fellowship would be disproportionate upwards and would undermine the credibility of the claims it makes about achievable outputs. The measures described in this sub-section are proportionate in the sense that each claimed outcome or impact is traceable to a specific deliverable and a specific mechanism, and none requires assumptions about outputs or events that go beyond what the project can produce within its confirmed scope and timeline.

The concrete actions can be organised into three phases:

During months 1–6 (establishment phase): the Data Management Plan (D5-01) and the Dissemination and exploitation plan (D5-02) are delivered, establishing the open-science framework prospectively. The Career Development Plan (D4-01, month 3) is delivered simultaneously, providing the framework for the fellow's communication training under the MSCA-PF mandatory transferable-skills dimensions — including the specific requirement of SR-03 that training activities foster open science and knowledge valorisation. The month-6 deliverables establish the entire dissemination, exploitation and communication governance structure before any primary research output exists.

During months 7–20 (active research and progressive dissemination phase): the Diagnostic model specification and calibration report (D1-01) is delivered at month 14 with its accompanying open-source code repository (KPI-05, KPI-10). Conference presentations at ISPRS, IEEE IGARSS and precision agriculture venues begin from month 14 onwards. The Decision engine and demonstrator software (D2-01) is delivered at month 20 with its accompanying open-source release (KPI-06). Curriculum integration of D1-01 outputs into ELTE's geoinformatics teaching is initiated from month 18 (KPI-10, KPI-11). The D5-02 dissemination plan is updated as WP1 and WP2 outputs materialise.

During months 21–24 and post-project (closure and sustainability phase): the Field validation dataset and uncertainty calibration report (D3-01) is delivered at month 24 with its FAIR-compliant open release under a persistent DOI or repository reference (KPI-08). Final publications from WP3 are prepared and submitted. The open research infrastructure — D1-01 code, D2-01 software, D3-01 benchmark dataset — is established in publicly accessible repositories and integrated into ELTE's ongoing research and teaching programme, providing the post-project sustainability foundation described in the Phase 5 sustainability mechanism.

The consolidated mapping of the dissemination, exploitation and communication measures to the seven call expected impacts (EI-01 through EI-07) is as follows. EI-02 (increased and broadened R&I impact through enhanced networking and communication) is realised through open-access publication of all WP1–WP3 outputs (D5-01, D5-02) combined with the fellow's communication training in WP4 (D4-01), delivering the project's substantive R&I content to the widest possible scientific and practitioner audience. EI-03 (stronger R&I capacity and output among participating organisations and better transfer of knowledge) is realised through the open-source code and benchmark dataset releases (D1-01, D2-01, D3-01) and the institutional research capacity building at Eötvös Loránd University (ELTE), Budapest through both technology outputs and the fellow-to-host knowledge transfer of non-destructive physiological measurement competence documented in D4-01. EI-04 (increased global attractiveness, visibility and reputation of the participating organisation and the ERA) is realised through open publication addressing the documented literature gap (real-time decision-support × PlanetScope, METH-SOTA-007) and the FAIR-released benchmark dataset (D3-01, KPI-08) that positions ELTE internationally in the precision agriculture sensing community. EI-06 (regular feedback of research results into teaching and education) is realised through the curriculum integration of D1-01 and D2-01 open-source outputs into ELTE's geoinformatics and remote sensing teaching from month 18, confirmed through KPI-10 and KPI-11. EI-01, EI-05 and EI-07 are primarily realised through the career-development and knowledge-transfer mechanisms addressed in sub-section 2.1, but are reinforced by the dissemination, exploitation and communication activities documented here to the extent that communication competences (D4-01, WP4 SR-03 training), open-science practices (D5-01, D5-02) and international networking through conference dissemination (D5-02, WP5) are components of the fellow's career development programme.

All six confirmed deliverables of the project — D1-01, D2-01, D3-01, D4-01, D5-01, D5-02 — are active instruments of the dissemination, exploitation and communication strategy at different scales and for different audiences. This integration of dissemination, exploitation and communication into the project's deliverable structure rather than as a parallel administrative track is the characteristic that makes the measures both proportionate and credible: they do not require additional effort beyond what the project must produce anyway, and they create lasting open infrastructure whose value to the scientific and practitioner communities persists well beyond the 24-month fellowship timeline.

sub_sections.title: The magnitude and importance of the project's contribution to the expected scientific, societal and economic impacts
sub_sections.content:
2.3  The magnitude and importance of the project's contribution to the expected scientific, societal and economic impacts

This sub-section addresses the third Impact sub-criterion: what the magnitude and importance of the project's contribution to the expected scientific, societal and economic impacts is, and how those results make a difference beyond the immediate scope of the fellowship. The account is organised in nine parts that follow the evaluator's analytical frame: (i) the principle for calibrating magnitude to a 24-month European Fellowship at TRL 3–4, and why that calibration is the precondition for honest impact claims; (ii) the scientific magnitude of filling the identified literature gap and what that means at the level of the research community, not only the project; (iii) the calibration standard as a lasting methodological contribution that extends beyond this project into a broader field; (iv) the open benchmark dataset as a community multiplier whose scientific value accumulates independently of the project team; (v) the economic and societal magnitude of the WUE-framed decision support architecture and the pathway from TRL 3–4 prototype to applied value; (vi) the environmental magnitude of the Route B landscape-compatible sensing principle and its reach beyond tomato horticulture; (vii) the ERA-level and institutional magnitude of the research capacity built at Eötvös Loránd University (ELTE), Budapest; (viii) the consolidated magnitude and importance dimension of each of the seven call expected impacts; and (ix) an explicit statement of what this project does not claim, and why that restraint is itself an indicator of scientific quality that an evaluator should weigh positively.


2.3.1  The right frame for magnitude: leverage-point impacts at TRL 3–4

The magnitude and importance of a research fellowship's contribution must be assessed within the correct causal model. A 24-month European Fellowship producing a research prototype at a confirmed TRL target of TRL 3–4 (RQ10) does not create its impacts through direct operational deployment, commercial uptake, or field-scale management change. It creates them through the leverage that a well-designed, openly validated, calibrated proof-of-concept exerts on the subsequent development pipeline. The relevant question is therefore not what the project deploys but what constraint it removes from subsequent actors who have the resources, institutional relationships, and timelines to carry the work from TRL 3–4 to operational status.

This distinction is not a concession to modesty; it is a claim about where the highest-leverage interventions in the multi-sensor probabilistic crop-water-state estimation research field currently sit. The binding constraint on the field's development is not the existence of sensors — Sentinel-1 SAR, Sentinel-2 optical and PlanetScope (access confirmed secured via the Planet platform and API, RQ8) are available to any researcher — nor the existence of crop models — FAO AquaCrop is openly documented — nor the existence of Bayesian methods for uncertainty propagation. The binding constraint is the absence of an openly available, FAIR-compliant, end-to-end reference implementation that couples multi-sensor probabilistic fusion to crop-water-state estimation to uncertainty-aware decision optimisation, validated against a rigorous calibration criterion on a publicly accessible benchmark dataset. No such reference implementation currently exists in the reviewed literature — as established by the Research Gap Matrix (METH-SOTA-007) covering fifty studies, which identifies the real-time decision-support × PlanetScope cell as empty. Creating that implementation, validating it against the 90% prediction-interval coverage criterion (RQ5), releasing all code and data openly under FAIR principles, and publishing the results in peer-reviewed open-access venues — this is the leverage-point intervention. The project's TRL 3–4 contribution directly addresses the binding constraint, which is why its magnitude is disproportionate to its scale and budget.

The importance of this framing for the evaluator is that it identifies the correct reference class for magnitude assessment. The appropriate comparator is not a large-scale operational precision agriculture deployment but the state of the literature and the open-source landscape in probabilistic multi-sensor crop-water sensing: what does this field need in order to advance, and does this project provide it? The answer, grounded in the identified literature gap and the project's confirmed open-infrastructure commitments, is yes.


2.3.2  Scientific magnitude: filling a specific gap and what that means at the community level

The scientific magnitude of the project's contribution rests on a specific, defended, and narrow claim: that the project fills the identified empty cell in the research-gap matrix for multi-sensor crop water stress monitoring — the intersection of real-time decision support and PlanetScope integration — with an end-to-end probabilistic architecture (IMP-1: Scientific advance in probabilistic multi-sensor crop-water-state estimation) that is genuinely novel in its end-to-end coupling of three elements: learned multimodal fusion directly from multiple sensor streams; explicit probabilistic crop-water-state estimation outputs carrying honest uncertainty; and water-use-efficiency-oriented irrigation decision optimisation drawing on those probabilistic estimates through counterfactual simulation over weather ensembles.

The importance of filling this specific gap, rather than the general importance of satellite data for agriculture, operates at three levels that are each worth assessing individually.

First, the existence-proof dimension. The scientific community working on multi-sensor crop-water-state estimation has access to all the technical components needed to build an honest end-to-end probabilistic pipeline. The gap is integrative, not component-level: no openly available, reproducible implementation has yet assembled the components with honest uncertainty propagation through the full pipeline and validated the result against a calibration criterion — as distinct from the accuracy-percentage and root-mean-square-error metrics that dominate current evaluations in the field. Once the existence proof exists and is openly available as confirmed through the project's FAIR release commitments under the Data Management Plan (D5-01: Data Management Plan, month 6, WP5: Dissemination, exploitation, communication and management), subsequent researchers and developers do not need to reconstruct the pipeline architecture from scratch. They can extend, adapt, challenge, and improve on a known working baseline rather than re-solving the integration problem. The leverage effect of an existence proof on a research community is well understood: it changes the epistemology from 'can this be done?' to 'what is the best way to do it?', which substantially reduces the activation energy for the field's subsequent development.

Second, the calibration quality-standard dimension, which is treated in full in sub-section 2.3.3 below as the most distinctive and transferable of the project's methodological contributions.

Third, the open reproducibility-infrastructure dimension. The research-gap matrix's finding that the real-time decision-support × PlanetScope cell is empty is not only a finding about the depth of the science — it is implicitly a finding about the scarcity of open reference implementations through which other researchers can study, replicate, and extend the methods. The project's commitment to open-source code releases alongside each technical deliverable — the diagnostic model code at month 14 (D1-01: Diagnostic model specification and calibration report), the decision engine and demonstrator software at month 20 (D2-01: Decision engine and demonstrator software), and the benchmark field-validation dataset at month 24 (D3-01: Field validation dataset and uncertainty calibration report) — creates reproducibility infrastructure that the community currently lacks. The scientific magnitude of this reproducibility contribution is distinct from, and potentially larger than, the direct publication impact of the project: every researcher who uses the project's open code to conduct a follow-on study on a different crop, sensor configuration, or geographic context produces new knowledge that traces back to the project's open infrastructure as a foundational resource. The community multiplier effect of FAIR-compliant open code and benchmark data in a domain where such resources are scarce is a well-established dynamic in computational science, and it means the project's impact accumulates beyond the citation lifetime of its initial publications.

The expected outcomes most directly advanced by the scientific magnitude dimension are EO-06 (Increased global attractiveness, visibility and reputation of the participating organisations) and EO-07 (Stronger R&I capacity and output among participating organisations; better transfer of knowledge), consistent with the Phase 5 impact architecture's confirmed pathways PWY-EI-03 and PWY-EI-04.


2.3.3  The calibration standard as a lasting methodological contribution beyond this project

The confirmed uncertainty-calibration criterion (RQ5: 90% prediction intervals contain the ground truth approximately 90% of the time on the validation set) and the confirmed pilot success criterion (RQ7: the RQ5 calibration target is met on the validation set) constitute more than a technical evaluation metric for this project. They constitute a methodological position on what scientific adequacy means for probabilistic crop-water-state estimation systems — a position that has importance beyond the immediate scope of the fellowship.

The importance of this methodological position at the community level derives from a well-known problem in probabilistic machine learning applied to environmental sensing: models can be accurate on average while being systematically overconfident in their uncertainty estimates. A model that reports 90% prediction intervals that in practice contain the ground truth only 60% of the time is not miscalibrated in a minor technical sense — it is providing false confidence to any decision-maker who relies on those intervals to characterise the risk of an irrigation decision. For a grower deciding whether to irrigate based on a probabilistic crop-water-state diagnosis, a systematically overconfident model does not merely underperform: it misrepresents the uncertainty that should govern the decision. The consequences of false confidence in an irrigation context are concrete: over-irrigation when the model reports false certainty that the crop is unstressed, and under-irrigation when it reports false certainty that soil moisture is adequate. Neither consequence is trivial under water-constrained conditions.

The project's calibration criterion (RQ5) addresses this problem at its source by requiring the system's stated uncertainty intervals to be honest in a well-defined, measurable sense before the pilot is considered successful (RQ7). This is a higher standard than accuracy-percentage validation, and it is a standard with transferable importance: any subsequent probabilistic crop-water-state estimation system that claims to support irrigation decisions should be able to demonstrate calibration evidence of the same kind, and the project's validation study in WP3 (Field validation, ground truth and uncertainty calibration) provides the methodological template for how such evidence should be collected and assessed.

The methodological template is embodied in the Field validation dataset and uncertainty calibration report (D3-01, month 24): non-destructive physiological ground truth (chlorophyll fluorescence, stomatal conductance, canopy/leaf temperature and spectral reflectance; RQ4) collected at co-located Hungarian tomato farm sites accessed via AgroVIR (Hungary) through the growing season, matched to multi-sensor EO observations from Sentinel-1 SAR, Sentinel-2 optical, PlanetScope and ERA5 meteorological reanalysis, and used to assess whether the diagnostic model's prediction intervals satisfy the 90% coverage criterion. The richness of the ground-truth characterisation — four physiological variables rather than a single spectral-index proxy — reflects Dr. Rositsa Cholakova's specialist expertise in exactly these instruments and is the quality differentiator that makes the calibration evidence in D3-01 scientifically credible for the crop physiology and precision agriculture communities, not just statistically adequate for a machine-learning evaluation benchmark.

Beyond this project, the calibration quality standard contributes to the growing movement in probabilistic EO and precision agriculture research toward calibrated evaluation rather than accuracy-only evaluation. A single fellowship that demonstrates the calibration criterion's practical feasibility and releases the validation protocol openly does not transform that movement, but it provides an example and a reproducible baseline from which the movement can build. The importance of this contribution is proportionate to the scarcity of calibration-validated precision agriculture systems in the current literature — which is, per the research-gap matrix (METH-SOTA-007), considerable.


2.3.4  The open benchmark dataset as a community multiplier

The Field validation dataset and uncertainty calibration report (D3-01, month 24), to be released openly under FAIR principles with a persistent identifier (DOI or open repository reference) as confirmed through KPI-08 in the Phase 5 impact architecture and governed by the Data Management Plan (D5-01, month 6), constitutes an independently valuable scientific contribution whose magnitude extends substantially beyond the fellowship period through a specific mechanism: it enables independent replication.

The value of an independently replicable benchmark in a research domain derives from the following dynamic. A research community in which every group validates its methods on privately generated, non-released data is a community in which methodological claims cannot be compared against a common standard: a model that performs well on one group's data may perform differently on another group's data for reasons that are indistinguishable from genuine methodological differences. The introduction of a public benchmark dataset with a defined ground-truth protocol and a defined calibration criterion creates the conditions for cumulative, comparable science: each successive methodological contribution can be evaluated against the same validation data, the same ground truth, and the same calibration standard, making genuine methodological progress distinguishable from artefacts of evaluation heterogeneity. In the domain of probabilistic multi-sensor crop-water-state estimation, where no such public benchmark currently exists for the tomato horticultural context, D3-01 fills this gap and provides the community infrastructure it requires.

The physiological ground-truth richness of D3-01 is a secondary magnitude argument. Chlorophyll fluorescence, stomatal conductance, canopy/leaf temperature and spectral reflectance (RQ4) together provide a multi-variable physiological characterisation of crop water status that is substantially more informative than the spectral-index proxies or yield records typically used as ground truth in satellite-based crop-water monitoring evaluations. This physiological richness makes D3-01 a richer resource for other researchers than a narrower ground-truth protocol would: it allows future users to assess their models against multiple physiological dimensions of the crop's water response, not only against a single surface-reflectance-derived proxy. The scientific value of the dataset to the community therefore exceeds what the project itself uses it for.

D3-01 also carries the Route B covariation evidence as an embedded methodological contribution. The confirmed co-located seasonal measurement campaign (RQ9: measuring the target tomato crop and the proxy patch simultaneously and demonstrating statistical covariation) is documented in D3-01 as both a result (does the covariation hypothesis hold in the Hungarian tomato context?) and a template (how should a covariation test be designed and executed for Route B validation in any context?). The template function — how to design and execute a co-located covariation campaign to test the homogeneous-patch-proxy assumption — is transferable to any agricultural landscape context where Route B's approach might be considered. Its documentation in a FAIR-compliant, openly accessible dataset report means that subsequent researchers need not rediscover the measurement design from scratch, which is a form of scientific efficiency that compounds over time as Route B's approach is considered for application in other contexts.

The durable standing of D3-01 as a scientific resource — accumulating dataset citations from researchers who use it for subsequent validation studies, accumulating methodological influence from researchers who adapt the calibration protocol, and accumulating impact on ELTE's international reputation through the KPI-08 persistent identifier — is the form of post-fellowship sustainability that is most characteristic of a well-designed open-infrastructure fellowship contribution. It continues to produce scientific value without requiring the project team's continued engagement.


2.3.5  Economic and societal magnitude: the WUE-framed decision support architecture and its pathway to applied value

The economic and societal magnitude of the project (IMP-2: Economic and societal impact: water-use efficiency and farm resilience) is realised through a specific architectural choice whose importance extends beyond the Hungarian tomato context in which it is validated.

The confirmed decision objective — water-use efficiency (RQ6) — is not a generic proxy for agricultural value. It is a choice about the appropriate objective function for irrigation decision support under water-constrained conditions. A WUE-framed decision support architecture recommends the irrigation decision that maximises the ratio of crop output to water applied, not the decision that maximises yield regardless of water cost. Under conditions where water is the scarce resource — conditions that are increasingly prevalent in Central European horticulture as summer rainfall variability increases and groundwater extraction faces regulatory pressure — a WUE-framed recommendation and a yield-maximising recommendation diverge systematically: the WUE-framed recommendation is more conservative in water application when the marginal yield response to additional water is small, and more assertive when the crop faces acute deficit that would cause disproportionate yield loss per unit of unirrigated stress. This systematic divergence is precisely the decision intelligence that practitioners need when water is constrained and the cost of each irrigation decision extends beyond the immediate energy and water purchase cost to longer-term impacts on water resource availability.

The architecture that implements this WUE objective is the uncertainty-aware AquaCrop calibration retaining an honest parameter posterior (OUT-2: Uncertainty-aware AquaCrop decision engine, confirmed in outcomes.json) combined with counterfactual irrigation simulation over weather ensembles. The counterfactual-over-ensembles approach implements the WUE objective under genuine uncertainty: the system generates a distribution of plausible weather futures, evaluates the WUE of each candidate irrigation decision across that distribution, and selects the decision whose expected WUE performance is most robust to the weather uncertainty the farmer faces. This is not a simplification of the decision problem — it is an accurate representation of the epistemic structure of an irrigation decision made before the growing-season weather is known. Its importance to the practitioner is that the resulting recommendation does not pretend to know the weather: it explicitly accounts for the range of weather scenarios and selects the most defensible irrigation choice given that range.

At the project scale, the demonstrator (D2-01: Decision engine and demonstrator software, month 20) exercises this architecture on Hungarian tomato farm conditions accessed via AgroVIR (Hungary) and delivers WUE-optimised recommendations alongside stated uncertainty intervals. No quantified water savings or yield improvements are asserted during the fellowship period: the project operates at TRL 3–4 (RQ10) and pilot success is defined as the calibration target being met (RQ7), not as a measurable agronomic outcome at field scale. What is demonstrated is that the architecture for quantifying WUE trade-offs under uncertainty — the counterfactual simulation, the parameter posterior, the weather-ensemble scoring — is feasible, implemented, validated for calibrated uncertainty (RQ5 criterion in WP3), and available openly for subsequent development.

At the beyond-project scale, the importance of the confirmed architecture is structural: agri-tech developers, public extension services, and precision agriculture platform operators seeking to build uncertainty-aware irrigation decision support — in Hungary, in Bulgaria, elsewhere in the EU — will, after this project, have access to an openly documented, validated reference architecture that they currently lack. The project's economic and societal contribution is not the WUE savings it delivers during the fellowship but the template it provides for systems that will deliver those savings at scale after the fellowship. This is the correct framing of economic importance at TRL 3–4, and it is grounded in the project's confirmed deliverable structure, confirmed data access (RQ8), and confirmed open IPR strategy under the Data Management Plan (D5-01).

AgroVIR's engagement throughout WP3 (Field validation, ground truth and uncertainty calibration) is the mechanism that grounds the demonstrator's design in the practical realities of the practitioner context during the fellowship period itself. AgroVIR's confirmed scope — farmer access, field validation support and iterative feedback, not ownership or operation of the tool — is precisely calibrated to the TRL 3–4 stage: it gives the research prototype real-world grounding and practitioner-informed design without asserting a deployment relationship that does not yet exist. The iterative feedback loop between the demonstrator's WUE recommendation outputs and AgroVIR's farming and agronomic advisory context is the societal relevance mechanism that operates within the fellowship's confirmed scope.


2.3.6  Environmental magnitude: the landscape-compatible sensing principle and its reach

Route B — the homogeneous patch proxy, confirmed as the project's primary route (RQ2) — carries an environmental co-benefit (IMP-3: Environmental co-benefit through landscape-compatible sensing) whose magnitude is grounded in a specific observation about the methodology's relationship to landscape composition.

Route B's core principle is that the sub-pixel resolution problem inherent in reading heterogeneous agricultural landscapes with coarse-resolution satellite instruments can be sidestepped by identifying a nearby, spectrally and biologically homogeneous patch — typically semi-natural or extensively managed vegetation — whose biological response to water stress co-varies with the target tomato crop. The coarse satellite pixel reads this patch cleanly, without the signal-mixing problems that arise when a heterogeneous pixel includes soil, canopy, and shadow in unpredictable proportions.
