The methodological logic therefore creates a direct instrumental argument for the presence of semi-natural or extensively managed patches in the agricultural landscape: they are precision-agriculture assets, not irrelevant externalities to be tolerated or eliminated.

The environmental magnitude of this argument is best understood at two scales. At the field scale, the Route B methodology provides an argument internal to the precision agriculture logic — not external to it via conservation regulations or biodiversity incentive schemes — for retaining or establishing compatible plant communities adjacent to intensively managed tomato fields. The precision-agriculture practitioner who deploys Route B benefits from the presence of a homogeneous proxy patch, which creates an ongoing instrumental incentive for landscape-compatible management that is self-sustaining as long as the technology is in use. This is a qualitatively different mechanism from regulatory compliance: it aligns economic and environmental incentives rather than placing them in tension.

The confirmed co-located seasonal measurement campaign (RQ9) validates this argument empirically by simultaneously measuring the target tomato crop and the proxy patch across the growing season and demonstrating their statistical covariation. The covariation demonstration in D3-01 (Field validation dataset and uncertainty calibration report, month 24) is the empirical evidence that the landscape-compatible sensing principle is not only theoretically plausible but operationally confirmed under real Hungarian tomato farm conditions. Its documentation as a FAIR-released dataset establishes the empirical basis on which other researchers can assess whether the same principle holds in other agricultural landscapes — brassica rotations, legume systems, other solanum species — where homogeneous semi-natural patches may co-vary with target crops in analogous ways. The project makes no claims about Route B's applicability in these other contexts beyond what has been validated in the Hungarian tomato setting; what it provides is the methodological template — the co-located covariation campaign design — for how that validation should be conducted. The reach of IMP-3's environmental argument beyond tomato horticulture is therefore a methodological reach rather than an asserted application reach, which is the appropriate framing at TRL 3–4.

The importance of IMP-3 relative to IMP-1 and IMP-2 is that it represents an environmental dimension of the project that arises from the methodological design choice (RQ2: Route B) rather than from a separate environmental objective. The project does not need to add an environmental component to its research agenda to realise IMP-3: it arises from the primary research design and is validated by the same co-located measurement campaign that validates Route B's technical performance. This integration of environmental benefit into the technical research design is a characteristic of methodological choices that the evaluator can assess as genuinely embedded, rather than appended.


2.3.7  ERA-level and institutional magnitude: building durable capacity at Eötvös Loránd University (ELTE), Budapest

The call's expected impact EI-03 (Stronger R&I capacity and output among participating organisations and better transfer of knowledge between participating organisations) addresses the institutional dimension of MSCA fellowship magnitude. The magnitude of this project's contribution to EI-03 at Eötvös Loránd University (ELTE), Budapest is greater than the sum of its three technical deliverables because it combines research capacity addition with validated methodology, open infrastructure, and the acquisition of a specialist competence — non-destructive physiological ground-truth measurement for agricultural EO validation — that the geoinformatics group does not currently hold.

Through WP1 (Probabilistic multi-sensor diagnosis of the field state) and WP2 (Uncertainty-aware decision engine and demonstrator integration), ELTE's Faculty of Informatics, Institute of Cartography and Geoinformatics acquires documented and validated research capacity in three methodological domains: (i) Bayesian multi-sensor calibration for heterogeneous EO inputs (Sentinel-1, Sentinel-2, PlanetScope, ERA5), anchored in D1-01 (Diagnostic model specification and calibration report, month 14); (ii) uncertainty-aware crop-model calibration retaining an honest parameter posterior and counterfactual decision simulation over weather ensembles, anchored in D2-01 (Decision engine and demonstrator software, month 20); and (iii) non-destructive physiological measurement protocol design, execution and calibration assessment for agricultural EO validation, transferred from Dr. Rositsa Cholakova's specialist expertise through WP4 (Training, supervision and two-way transfer of knowledge) and documented in the Career Development Plan (D4-01, month 3). The third capacity addition — non-destructive physiological measurement — is the one that persists most distinctively in ELTE's research infrastructure after the fellowship ends: it is the competence that ELTE's geoinformatics group currently does not hold at the operational level and that the two-way knowledge transfer structure of this fellowship makes available to the group permanently, not only for the duration of the action.

The open FAIR release of all primary research software (D1-01 code at month 14, D2-01 software at month 20) and the benchmark dataset (D3-01 at month 24) under the Data Management Plan (D5-01) anchors this capacity in publicly accessible, reproducible artefacts that ELTE researchers and students can use and extend without dependence on the fellow's continued presence. The integration of the D1-01 and D2-01 open-source outputs into ELTE's geoinformatics and remote-sensing teaching curricula from month 18 — as confirmed in the Phase 5 exploitation plan and evidenced through KPI-10 (open code repository established at D1-01 delivery, FAIR compliance confirmed by D5-01) and KPI-11 (D5-01 by month 6 covering all WP1–WP3 data assets) — further embeds the project's research contribution into ELTE's institutional functioning beyond the fellowship period, realising the call's expected impact EI-06 (Regular feedback of research results into teaching and education at participating organisations) through a structural rather than opportunistic mechanism: ELTE is a university host with active geoinformatics, remote sensing and precision agriculture curricula, so the teaching feedback loop is built into the host-type, not bolted on.

At the ERA level, the project's contribution to EI-04 (Increased global attractiveness, visibility and reputation of the participating organisation and the European Research Area) is grounded in the combination of open publication addressing the documented gap (real-time decision-support × PlanetScope, METH-SOTA-007) and the FAIR-released benchmark dataset D3-01 positioned explicitly as an internationally reproducible resource. The magnitude of ELTE's reputational contribution from this project derives from the specificity of the gap addressed: filling a documented empty cell in a fifty-study research-gap matrix with a calibrated, openly reproducible implementation creates a citable scientific reference point that international researchers in the domain will recognise and cite, because it provides something they need and currently do not have. This is more targeted reputational impact than generic conference presence, and it is the appropriate mechanism for a 24-month fellowship to build ELTE's international standing in multi-sensor EO and precision agriculture — verified through KPI-07 (D5-02 by month 6 with international open-access venues identified for WP1 and WP2 outputs) and KPI-08 (D3-01 released with persistent identifier by month 24).


2.3.8  Consolidated magnitude and importance dimension of the seven call expected impacts

The seven call expected impacts are each covered by confirmed project pathways (coverage_status = Covered for all seven per the Phase 5 impact architecture, impact_architecture.json). The following consolidation addresses specifically the magnitude and importance dimension of each coverage — what is the scale of the contribution and why does it matter beyond the immediate project — complementing rather than repeating the pathway narratives and KPI structure established in the Phase 5 impact architecture.

EI-01 (Improved employability and career prospects of MSCA postdoctoral fellows within academia and beyond): the magnitude of the project's contribution rests on the structural rarity of the competence profile it creates. The coupling of practised non-destructive stress phenotyping in tomato horticulture — grounded in a summa cum laude doctoral thesis and approximately four years of post-doctoral specialist practice — with geoinformatics, Bayesian multi-sensor calibration, and uncertainty-aware crop modelling is rare in both the precision agriculture and the Earth observation research communities. It is important beyond the immediate scope because it creates a research voice that is positioned to contribute credibly at the intersection of physiological ground truth and probabilistic EO estimation, a position that neither a pure physiologist nor a pure EO researcher can occupy — and the precision agriculture research field demonstrably needs researchers who can bridge these two validation registers. The verifiable indicators are KPI-01 (D4-01: Career Development Plan submitted by month 3, covering all MSCA-PF mandatory training dimensions) and KPI-02 (both transfer directions documented in CDP reviews).

EI-02 (Increased and broadened R&I impact through enhanced networking and communication): the magnitude derives from the three primary deliverables each addressing a distinct and independently publishable dimension of the literature gap — probabilistic fusion methodology (D1-01), uncertainty-aware decision engine (D2-01), and calibration validation study (D3-01) — rather than a single publication on a broad topic. Three distinct publications addressing specific technical communities (multi-sensor EO, uncertainty-aware crop modelling, calibration methodology) cumulatively produce broader R&I impact than a single general contribution. The importance beyond the immediate project is that the fellow's cross-disciplinary position gives her a distinctive voice in both the EO and precision agriculture publication communities for subsequent work in the field, compounding the initial publications' impact. KPI-03 (D5-01 by month 6 covering all primary data assets under FAIR principles) and KPI-04 (D5-02 by month 6 with confirmed open-access routes for WP1–WP3 outputs) are the verifiable indicators.

EI-03 (Stronger R&I capacity and output): the magnitude derives from the combination of three new openly available methodological contributions (probabilistic fusion diagnostic model, uncertainty-aware decision engine, benchmark field-validation dataset) with the acquisition by Eötvös Loránd University (ELTE), Budapest of non-destructive physiological measurement competence — a specialist capability that the geoinformatics group does not currently hold. The importance is that the acquired competence and open infrastructure are precisely aligned with the methodological directions in which ELTE's future precision agriculture research programme is most limited, so the capacity additions are high-leverage at the institutional level. KPI-05 (D1-01 by month 14 with calibration evidence) and KPI-06 (D2-01 by month 20 as open-source software with WUE-based decision logic documented) are the verifiable indicators.

EI-04 (Increased attractiveness, visibility and reputation): the magnitude derives from the specificity of the scientific contribution — filling a documented empty cell in a research-gap matrix — and from the FAIR-released benchmark dataset (D3-01) as a citable, internationally reproducible resource. The importance is that specific gap-filling contributions are more visible and more durably citable than generic methodological contributions, because the community recognises and acknowledges the gap being closed and has an instrumental reason to cite and use the work. KPI-07 (D5-02 by month 6 with international venues identified for WP1 and WP2 outputs) and KPI-08 (D3-01 with persistent identifier by month 24) are the verifiable indicators.

EI-05 (Increased alignment with European Charter for Researchers principles): the magnitude derives from the Career Development Plan (D4-01, month 3) jointly prepared within a supervisory relationship where Dr. András Jung holds habilitations in both Computer Science and Crop Sciences, providing Charter-aligned specialist authority across both disciplinary dimensions of the fellowship from a single supervisor rather than distributing that authority across a supervisory committee. The importance is that Charter alignment is most consequential when the supervision is substantively expert in the fellow's actual research domain — which this supervisory structure delivers for both the probabilistic modelling and the agronomic interpretation dimensions of the project. KPI-09 (D4-01 assessed against Charter dimensions) is the verifiable indicator.

EI-06 (Regular feedback of research results into teaching and education): the magnitude derives from the open-source code releases (D1-01 code at month 14, D2-01 software at month 20) constituting concrete, executable, FAIR-compliant teaching materials rather than static publications. The importance is structural: ELTE is a university host with active geoinformatics, remote sensing and precision agriculture teaching at MSc and PhD level, so the curriculum integration pathway from research output to teaching use is short, reliable, and institutional rather than incidental. KPI-10 and KPI-11 are the verifiable indicators, confirming FAIR compliance and open availability from the point of each technical deliverable's release.

EI-07 (New mind-sets through interdisciplinary experience): the magnitude is grounded in the concrete scientific product of the interdisciplinary approach — the probabilistic fusion methodology (D1-01) — which integrates plant-physiology-grounded ground-truth design with Bayesian multi-sensor estimation in a combination that neither the physiological nor the EO discipline alone would have produced. The importance is that the new mind-set is evidenced by a scientific output, not merely asserted: the Diagnostic model specification and calibration report (D1-01) contains design choices that are traceable to the fellow's plant-physiology expertise — the choice of non-destructive physiological ground-truth instruments (RQ4), the calibration quality standard (RQ5), the Route B patch-covariation test (RQ9) — and to the host's geoinformatics expertise — the Bayesian multi-sensor fusion architecture, the uncertainty propagation methodology. Their synthesis in a single deliverable is the evidence that the interdisciplinary combination produced something neither discipline alone could have produced, which is the correct meaning of 'new mind-sets' at the output level. KPI-12 and KPI-13 are the verifiable indicators.


2.3.9  What this project does not claim, and why that restraint is a positive evaluator signal

A complete and honest magnitude account for this project requires a clear statement of what it does not claim. The most common failure mode in research fellowship impact narratives is overclaiming — asserting impacts that belong to the operational deployment stages lying beyond the fellowship's scope, not to the research prototype it actually produces. The evaluator must assess whether the project's magnitude claims are credible and proportionate, and that assessment requires knowing not only what is claimed but what is explicitly not claimed.

This project does not claim: quantified field-scale water savings during the fellowship period; operational deployment of the decision engine as a commercial irrigation advisory service or public extension tool; yield improvements attributable to the project's interventions during the fellowship period; any form of commercial uptake or revenue generation from the demonstrator; integration of the demonstrator into AgroVIR's operational farm management services; or specific numeric career outcomes for Dr. Rositsa Cholakova — publication counts, training hours, thesis co-supervision numbers, or follow-on proposal deadlines — that were not operator-provided and that are to be specified jointly in the Career Development Plan (D4-01) with Dr. András Jung at the start of the action.

These claims are not made because they belong to stages of the pipeline — TRL 5 through TRL 9, operational system integration, commercial deployment, and long-term career measurement — that lie beyond the confirmed TRL target (TRL 3–4, RQ10) and the 24-month European Fellowship timeline. Asserting them would make the impact narrative disproportionate and epistemically dishonest. The pilot success criterion (RQ7) is defined precisely and honestly: the RQ5 calibration target is met on the validation set. Not 'the tool is adopted by Hungarian tomato growers.' Not 'water use on Hungarian tomato farms is reduced by X percent.' These would be outcomes of a successful operational deployment cycle that begins after TRL 3–4 is validated, not outcomes of the TRL 3–4 validation itself.

The importance of this restraint for the evaluator is two-fold. First, it makes the claims that are asserted more credible. A project that is explicit about what it does not claim, and why, gives the evaluator confidence that the claims it does make are grounded in the project's actual design and deliverables rather than in aspirational framing that cannot be verified against any deliverable. Second, the restraint itself is a scientific quality indicator: a project that defines its success criterion as meeting a calibration standard (RQ7 = RQ5 target met on the validation set) rather than as a vague commitment to agricultural transformation has internalised the same intellectual honesty that its central methodological commitment — the 90% prediction-interval coverage criterion (RQ5) — requires. A system that reports its own uncertainty honestly, and a proposal that reports its own scope honestly, are both expressions of the same scientific disposition. That consistency between methodological commitment and impact-claim scope is the correct marker of a well-designed scientific contribution at TRL 3–4.
